title: A reseed rebinds live sessions to the wrong people
description:
`private.session.person_id` holds `person.entity_id` from the main store, with
no foreign key — the two are separate databases (ADR 0003), and the column
comment says as much. `pnpm db:reseed` redraws every `entity_id`, which is
already documented: "`/people/722436` was Steve Lang in one promotion of the
sandbox's data and Robert Pederson in the next" (AGENTS.md).

Put together: **after a reseed, every surviving session resolves to whoever
inherited its number.** A signed-in volunteer is silently browsing and acting
as a different person — under `mine` scope, which is forced for volunteers, so
what they see is that person's samples. Session lookup
(`src/app/session.ts:68-73`) joins `session → person → inat_account → token`
and never checks that the person it landed on is the one the token belongs to,
so nothing catches it.

Measured on the sandbox, 2026-08-27, before today's reseed: 8 live sessions
across 6 people, and every person's id moved — AC Quinn 15525 → 15873,
Abigail Skoda 15831 → 16184. The reseed run today purged `session` by hand
before swapping the store, which is why nobody was rebound.

The runbook is wrong where it reassures: *"`private.duckdb` is untouched, so
sessions and volunteer tokens survive."* Tokens do — `inat_oauth_token` is
keyed by `inat_user_id`, which is stable. Sessions survive as stale pointers,
which is worse than not surviving.

Fixes worth weighing:

1. **Purge `session` as part of `db:reseed`.** Smallest, and correct: a
   session is a claim about a store that no longer exists. Everyone signs in
   again, which costs nothing because the OAuth token persists. Should live in
   the reseed path rather than in an operator's memory — today it was in mine.
2. **Key the session on something stable** — `inat_user_id`, or the login —
   and resolve the person at request time. Removes the class of bug rather
   than the instance, and is the same argument the roster already makes for
   addressing people by login rather than `entity_id` in URLs.
3. **Verify on read**: check the session's person still matches the token's
   `inat_user_id` and drop the session if not. Cheap belt-and-braces, and
   catches any other route to a stale id.

2 is the real fix; 1 should land immediately regardless, since it is a few
lines and removes the foot-gun from every future reseed. Also fix the runbook
sentence, which currently tells the next operator the opposite.

P0 because it is an authentication defect with a live trigger — the reseed
procedure is documented, expected to run repeatedly before cutover
("assume more before cutover, and check after any change under `ingest/`"),
and the correct step is currently nowhere but this bead.
close_reason: Fixed at the root rather than worked around: private.session now holds inat_user_id, which is iNaturalist's number and survives any rebuild of ours, and the person resolves through inat_account per request. A reseed is now invisible to sessions instead of silently rebinding them. Two behaviours fall out and are correct: unbinding an account ends its sessions, rebinding moves them. The private store is patched at boot beside the icon_url precedent — the old table is dropped rather than translated, since rewriting those rows would mean trusting the ids that were the bug, so everyone signs out exactly once with OAuth tokens intact. Deployed and verified on the sandbox: session is (id, inat_user_id, created_at, last_seen_at) and all 4 tokens survived. The manual purge added to the runbook mid-deploy is removed — it is no longer needed. Tests cover the renumbering case, unbinding, and the boot repair.

title: Legacy import would land ~271 stand-in coordinates as believed-true; re-measure at cutover
description:
Legacy samples would enter sample_location holding points iNaturalist published to hide the real ones, believed true. **The dump is re-fetched at cutover (Peter, 2026-09-22), so the figure that matters is production's at that moment: 271 specimens as of 2026-09-22, not the 1,641 in the 20 August staging.** Both measurements are kept below, because the gap between them is the evidence that the count tracks the dump's age rather than anything fixed — re-run the production measurement when the cutover dump is taken. sample_location is documented as believed-true coordinates and sample says outright that "deliberately-shifted (geoprivacy-obscured) coordinates never enter the sample layer" — but the legacy import lands every OBP-Server coordinate as legacy_import/believed-true. qc_rule_obscured_no_true_coordinates does not catch them: it fires when an obscured sample has no location row, and these have one.

## Count from Beeline's own sync, not from production's flags

An earlier version of this bead counted the 1,930 records production has flagged and called that "the whole flagged legacy population". It is not: the import takes its flags from Beeline's sync, and production's `geoprivacy`/`taxon_geoprivacy` fields only carry a value for records it has refreshed since that refresh shipped on 2026-08-30. In the 20 August legacy dump, **none of the 3,857 legacy rows whose observations Beeline sees as obscured carried a flag in production** — zero. Production's flag field is therefore a poor filter for "is this observation obscured", and the OBP-side figure of 271 undercounts by roughly six times.

Measured on a copy of `beeline.duckdb` (legacy fetch 20 August, observations synced with project trust), for legacy samples whose observation Beeline sees as obscured:

| verdict | samples | specimens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| stored pair equals the CURRENT public point | 233 | 885 |
| stored pair is an OLDER stand-in (>=5 km from the true point) | 132 | 756 |
| within 100 m of the true point — sound, must not be blanked | 152 | 2,055 |
| between 100 m and 5 km — ambiguous | 29 | 224 |
| no private point available to check against | 89 | 301 |

```sql
WITH legacy AS (
  SELECT s.entity_id, s.specimen_count, l.latitude, l.longitude,
         f.latitude flat, f.longitude flon, f.private_latitude plat, f.private_longitude plon
  FROM sample s
  JOIN sample_location l ON l.sample_id = s.entity_id
  JOIN observation_field f ON f.inat_id = s.inat_observation_id
  WHERE l.source = 'legacy_import'
    AND (nullif(f.geoprivacy,'open') IS NOT NULL OR nullif(f.taxon_geoprivacy,'open') IS NOT NULL)
), c AS (
  SELECT *,
    round(latitude,4)=round(flat,4) AND round(longitude,4)=round(flon,4) AS eq_public,
    CASE WHEN plat IS NULL THEN NULL
         ELSE 111.2*sqrt(power(latitude-plat,2)+power((longitude-plon)*cos(radians(plat)),2)) END AS km
  FROM legacy
)
SELECT CASE WHEN eq_public THEN '1 equals current public point'
            WHEN km IS NULL THEN '4 no private point available'
            WHEN km >= 5 THEN '2 older stand-in (>=5km)'
            WHEN km < 0.1 THEN '3 true (<100m)'
            ELSE '5 between 100m and 5km' END AS verdict,
       count(*) AS samples, sum(specimen_count) AS specimens
FROM c GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

## The test is the private point, not the public one

Comparing the stored pair to the observation's CURRENT public point finds the first row and silently passes the second, which is the dangerous part: iNaturalist republishes a different stand-in within the same obscuring cell when an observation's coordinates are edited, so a years-old stored stand-in no longer matches today's. Compare against `private_geojson` under project trust and treat anything beyond about 100 m as not-true. The giveaway for a stale stand-in is that it still falls in the same 0.2° cell as the true point, where a moved pin would scatter.

Two worked examples, both taxon-obscured:

- **Current stand-in** — OBA_2125556, label printed 31 December 2021, staged at 43.3780 -120.2870, locality "Christmas Valley". That is what api.inaturalist.org publishes today for observation 85187606.
- **Older stand-in** — OBA_2120952, staged at 43.2250 -120.3530, which is 10.8 km from the true point of observation 89222994 and inside the same 0.2° cell. Nothing about the stored pair looks wrong.

## Taxon-obscured coordinates are not permanently out of reach

An earlier version of this bead said no project-admin token would ever reveal the taxon-obscured ones. That is wrong, and Beeline's own store disproves it: it holds `private_geojson` for 199 of its 224 taxon-obscured-only observations (example: 399743567). Access appears to follow each observer's project-trust setting rather than the kind of obscuring, so the unreachable ones depend on settings that observers can change. The 89 samples above are those Beeline currently has no private point for, not a permanent floor.

## Production today says 271, and the gap is probably the staging's age

Measured on production 2026-09-22 with its own curator token, starting from iNaturalist's list of obscured observations in the three projects (18521, 99706, 166376) rather than from production's flags: 880 obscured observations, 867 of them returning a private point, 713 matched to occurrences, 4,132 specimens. Of those, 122 specimens hold the current stand-in and 149 an older one — **271 wrong, against 3,817 within 100 m of the true point, 4 ambiguous and 40 with no private point available**.

That is six times fewer than the 1,641 above, and the two are measured against different stores: this one against production as it stands, the table above against staging taken on 20 August. The likely explanation — a hypothesis, not a finding — is that production has since written true points into records whose coordinate access was granted (2,346 now carry `coordinateSource: private`), which the August staging predates. **Since the dump is re-fetched at cutover, this is the figure the import faces, and the August staging overstates it.** The population is also effectively frozen: an obscured record with no private point is flagged, never given a field number, and discarded at the end of the run, which is why production holds no obscured record with `coordinateSource: 'public'` at all. The script is `audit.mjs` in the 2026-09-22 OBP-Server session scratchpad; it decrypts the stored OAuth token in the worker container, exchanges it for an API token, pages the three projects and compares each occurrence to `private_geojson`.

## OBP-Server side, for cross-reference

An earlier pass filtered on production's own `geoprivacy`/`taxon_geoprivacy` fields, which covers only 1,930 records and 152 observations, and found 129 current stand-ins and 142 older ones. It reached the same 271 by a narrower route. Do not use production's flag fields as the filter — they only carry a value for records refreshed since 2026-08-30, which is why that pass saw 152 observations where iNaturalist reports 880.

## Upstream

oregon-bee-project/OBP-Server#59 stops OBP-Server storing these points at all and keeps them off labels, so the population is bounded and will not grow. It does not clean up what is stored, and that cleanup is unscheduled and may never run — OBP-Server is superseded by Beeline within a month or two, so this import should not assume it happened. What to do about the pinned labels, which will not be reprinted, is Arthur's decision and is open with him.

Both corrections above came from a Beeline session reviewing this bead; the errors were mine.

🤖

Loads are only stored when an observation's content changes, so an observation in two projects may be credited to just one of them.

```sql
WITH proj AS (
  SELECT l.inat_id, string_agg(DISTINCT r.source, ',' ORDER BY r.source) projects
  FROM observation_load l JOIN sync_run r ON r.entity_id = l.sync_run_id
  GROUP BY l.inat_id)
SELECT p.projects,
       CASE WHEN nullif(f.geoprivacy,'open') IS NOT NULL THEN 'observer' ELSE 'taxon only' END why_hidden,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE f.private_latitude IS NOT NULL) with_true_point,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE f.private_latitude IS NULL) no_true_point
FROM observation_field f JOIN proj p ON p.inat_id = f.inat_id
WHERE nullif(f.geoprivacy,'open') IS NOT NULL OR nullif(f.taxon_geoprivacy,'open') IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL;
```

title: Two requests on one session can collide: the session slide conflicts and the page is a 500
description: Found by bench/contention.ts (the 'one session' phase). cookieSessionResolver UPDATEs private.session.last_seen_at on every request. DuckDB has no row locks: when two requests carrying the same cookie overlap, the second UPDATE fails with 'TransactionContext Error: Conflict on update!' and the request answers 500. Measured: 3 of ~136 reads on the workstation, 1 of ~70 on the sandbox, with 4 concurrent readers on one cookie. In real use that is two tabs, a page and its CSV download, or a double click. Fix options: treat a conflict on the slide as success (somebody else just slid it, which is the same outcome); or throttle the slide the way person_activity already is. Either way the slide must never fail a read. Rerun pnpm bench:contention to confirm 'failed reads' is 0 in that phase.
close_reason: Fixed in #85 (b939c23): the session slide is throttled to five minutes and both resolver writes may lose a conflict. Burst test in test/auth.test.ts; bench:contention 'one session' phase at 0 failed reads.

title: A sample's window needs times: ten-minute net collections and six-hour pan traps
description: sample.date_start and date_end are dates. The BLM protocols record a start and a stop time for a ten-minute net collection, and a start and an end for a six-hour pan trap, both recorded rather than assumed. The reconcile key and qc_rule_duplicate_sample_number both group on date_start, so adding times touches them. Protocol becomes a controlled vocabulary for these samples, with effort fixed by the protocol rather than written into a free-text string. Cheapest before cutover.

title: Re-deriving a store records changes nobody made: the half-derived state between promotions lands in the change logs
description:
Re-deriving a deployed store writes tens of thousands of changes nobody made into the person and sample change logs, which are the authored history ADR 0007 exists to keep honest. Following the runbook's re-derivation procedure on Fly on 2026-09-15 appended 70,380 sample-log entries and 14 person-log entries, and every one of them was an artifact of the rebuild's intermediate state.

Example: a sample minted from an iNaturalist observation in August, and already in the log's baseline, was recorded again as though it had just been minted — every field going from nothing to a value — by observation promotion. And four people had their iNat account recorded as unbound by legacy promotion and bound again minutes later by observation promotion or the account backfill.

Why: the runbook exports BEELINE_DB as the new store for the whole sequence (legacy:promote, inat:promote, inat:backfill-accounts), and each of those steps runs a change pass against the log. Between legacy promotion and observation promotion the store is only half derived — observation-derived locations are gone and minted samples do not exist — and the sample pass restates its baseline (data/sample-state.csv) wholesale, so the next pass records everything coming back as new change. A sample falling silent records nothing, which is why the minted samples reappear as creations rather than as a move.

Measured on the appended rows: 48,482 sample entries cancel out within the run (24,241 sample-fields removed and restored, almost all location and location_source); the other 21,898 record 1,374 samples as newly minted, and all 1,374 were already in the pre-rebuild baseline. All 14 person entries cancel out. PR #59, the change being deployed, alters no field either log tracks, so the honest net was close to zero.

What was done this time: the three files were restored from the copy taken just before the rebuild (data/pre-reseed-20260915T023426Z on the volume), the polluted versions kept in data/post-reseed-* beside it, and the app's boot pass left to record whatever really differs, attributed to that pass.

Not decided: whether the change passes should run once, at the end of the whole derivation, or the runbook should stop exporting BEELINE_DB for the sequence and rely on the boot pass alone. Either way docs/runbooks/deploy-maderas.md "Re-deriving the model" currently prescribes the procedure that produces this, and says so as a feature ("each of them records, so it has to be set for the pair").
notes:
Outcome on Fly, 2026-09-15: after restoring the three files and swapping the rebuilt store in, the app's boot pass recorded 0 person changes and 39 sample changes, attributed to reconcile. Those 39 are real differences the re-derivation produced (for example an iNat host identification corrected since the last promotion, and a specimen count that went from 1 to 2), against the 70,394 entries the runbook's procedure had appended.
Fixed in the runbooks by PR #60 (https://github.com/rainhead/beeline/pull/60): the procedure no longer exports BEELINE_DB, so each promotion step records nothing and the app's first boot on the swapped-in store records the net difference once. The code alternative, one change pass at the end of the whole rebuild so entries stay attributed to promotion, is not taken.
close_reason: Merged in #60

title: Minting skips a long place name for the town behind it, so a sample's locality can name somewhere the bee was not, unflagged
description:
A sample minted from an iNaturalist observation can carry a locality naming a town kilometres from where the bee was collected, with no QC finding, so it would print that way on a permanent label. The reference implementation flags the same observation and makes the volunteer write the locality; minting here picks one silently.

Example: observation https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/396242867 (rainhead, 2026-08-31, sampleId 1). Its place_guess is "Deception Creek Trail, Skykomish, WA, US". observation_locality (schema/108_views_minting.sql) takes the first comma-separated component that reads like a place name and is at most 18 characters. "Deception Creek Trail" is 21, so it falls through to "Skykomish". The collecting point (47.7123, -121.1939, 3 m accuracy) is 12.3 km from Skykomish (iNat place 128701). On the dev store its sample has locality Skykomish and no QC finding of any kind.

What the reference does: parseLocalityFromPlaceGuess in OBP-Server (https://github.com/oregon-bee-project/OBP-Server/blob/main/shared/lib/services/OccurrenceService.js) takes the first component only when the guess has exactly three parts, and otherwise writes the whole guess in quotes, which its locality flag (commas, quotes, over 18 characters) catches. Blunt, but it refuses to guess, and here refusing was right.

How much (dev store, observations loaded through 2026-09-02): 113 observations had their first component skipped for length alone and a later one taken, 103 of them in the open season and 10 settled, so this is current practice and not residue. 18 samples carry the substituted locality (12 open season, 6 settled). The commonest: "Fremont-Winema National Forests" became Silver Lake (14), "Olympic National Park" Port Angeles (6), "Mt. Hood National Forest" Maupin, "Ankeny National Wildlife Refuge" Jefferson, "Deschutes National Forest" Sisters. A forest, park or refuge is not in the town its postal address names, so the substitute is wrong in exactly the way a label cannot afford.

Why the design missed it: the comment on observation_locality counts the trades the street-suffix change made (beeline-4dt), including two where a town replaced a road-derived name, but never the length refusal, which promotes the next component in the same way on every observation it touches.

Seen in the same rows, and not this bug: a Canadian postcode ("BC V0H 1T5") passes as a locality, because the postcode filter only knows five-digit US ZIPs; and a regional district ("Kootenay Boundary") is taken as one.

Not decided — Peter's call — is what minting should do when the component that names the place is too long for a label:
- mint the long component and let qc_rule_locality_format flag it as too long, so the volunteer shortens words that are at least about the right place;
- mint no locality, so the sample is flagged as missing one and the volunteer writes it upstream, which is the reference's outcome;
- keep substituting only where the later component is near the point, which needs a gazetteer this store does not have.
Whichever is chosen, the descriptive refresh is fill-only, so the samples already carrying a substituted locality keep it; they need their own repair or finding.
notes:
Decided (Peter, 2026-09-14): option (a). When the component that names the place is too long for a label, minting takes it anyway and qc_rule_locality_format flags it as too long, so the volunteer shortens words that are about the right place rather than inheriting a town somewhere else. The samples already carrying a substituted locality still need their own repair, since the descriptive refresh is fill-only.
Another shape observation_locality lets through, seen while redeploying on 2026-09-15: a Google plus code. One minted sample carried the locality 'MGF8+RH' until a re-derivation re-minted it from the observation's current place_guess ('Minidoka NWR'). Seven characters and no leading digit, so none of the rule's clauses refuse it, and on a label it names nothing a person can read. Same family as the Canadian postcode noted above; worth covering when this bug's rule is revisited.
Revised decision (Peter, 2026-09-15), replacing plain (a): take the long place name, and let an unprinted minted sample's locality follow its observation on every promotion until its labels print. Plain (a) could not work: iNat-linked samples are not editable in the app (src/app/sample-edit.ts) and the descriptive refresh was fill-only, so a locality_format finding on a minted sample could be cleared by nobody. Following upstream until print is the model decided in #58. Also found: the substitution is usually right for minted samples (9 of 10 are urban places inside the town), and a containment check through the observation's own iNat places does not separate right from wrong (community places and ecoregions match, many real towns have no place). Plus codes and Canadian postcodes are refused as localities in the same change.
Built 2026-09-15. Trial on a copy of the dev store (migrations 0027 and 0028, then inat:promote): 17 localities change, all open season and all unprinted; 9 become the long place name and are flagged by locality_format (3,890 -> 3,899 findings), 8 are corrected — MGF8+RH -> Minidoka, and seven upstream fixes the fill-only refresh never carried ('Sammamish Commons' -> Sammamish on six samples, 'Lake Vallely' -> Lake Valley). missing_required_field unchanged at 266; sample count unchanged. Deploy is fly deploy (0028 at boot) and the next promotion; no reseed.

title: Nightly data dump in the legacy system's format, for existing reporting
description:
Decided by Andony in the 2026-09-11 meeting: Beeline will export a dump of its data in the same format the legacy system produced, so the reporting systems already built on that dump keep working through cutover and after. This is separate from the recovery backups (beeline-elf), which staff never open.

The legacy system's canonical dump is workingOccurrences.csv. It holds every record as CSV, and the system uploaded it to Google Drive. It was its only automated outbound integration (docs/reference-implementation.md). The code that writes it is OBP-Server server/src/writeWorkingOccurrences.js, and worker/src/handlers/SyncOccurrencesSubtaskHandler.js shows how it was synced. Andony's R script for checking continuity between data pulls is one known consumer (docs/reference-implementation.md). There are probably others.

Cutover is the deadline. When the legacy system is frozen, its dump stops updating, and everything downstream silently goes stale.

Work:
- Pin down the format from the code, not from a sample file: the columns, their order, how dates are written (including Roman-numeral months), how names are put together, how blank values are written, and the encoding. An R script will break on any difference.
- Find every consumer, and ask whoever owns each one which columns they actually read. Matching every column exactly, including the legacy quirks, costs more than matching the columns someone reads.
- Decide what to do with columns Beeline has no equivalent for, and with things Beeline has that the legacy system had none of: qualifiers, per-row coordinate provenance, samples minted from iNaturalist. The rule is to stay format-compatible and add nothing new.
- As a test, put the dump next to the final legacy file from the cutover pull and check it row by row. The number of differences, split by season, is how we know it is done.

Questions:
- Where does it go? The same OSU/MM Drive, probably. It must not replace the file the legacy system is still writing until cutover.
- Does the per-atlas gate on volunteer determinations apply (beeline-pyr: any public view or export, to any system)? Or do internal reporting systems count as inside the program? And do taxon-obscured true coordinates go in? Presumably yes, since the legacy dump included them. Confirm both with Andony.
- Who owns the consumers, and are any of them public-facing?
notes:
The per-atlas gate question above is stale (2026-09-14). There is no gate inside Beeline: staff choose what to upload (beeline-pyr). The dump's consumers are internal reporting, so what remains is:
- Does it carry volunteer determinations, marked as such, the way the staff download does?
- Does it carry taxon-obscured true coordinates? Presumably yes, as the legacy dump did.

title: Nightly backups of the stores to Google Drive, ready by cutover
description:
Andony, meeting 2026-09-11: we want nightly backups to a Google Drive.

WHAT EXISTS: scripts/backup-authored-files.sh runs nightly from cron on maderas. It pulls the five authored CSVs off the Fly volume (corrections, both person files, both sample files), checks their hashes, and writes one ~1.7 MB tarball to maderas's local disk (docs/runbooks/deploy-fly.md, 'Backups'). It PULLS on purpose, so the Fly machine holds no credential for the backup host. Besides that, the volume has Fly's 14-day block snapshots, which Fly itself says are not a backup.

WHAT IS MISSING:
- beeline.duckdb is deliberately left out today, because it can be rebuilt by re-ingestion. After cutover that stops being true: minted field numbers, print runs, determinations entered in the app and staff overrides exist nowhere else. The roadmap already says backups become mandatory at cutover (phase 8) and that real backups start with export (phase 7).
- private.duckdb (ADR 0003). It now matters more, because Beeline manages mailing addresses itself (beeline-1kb.6, GitHub #34). ADR 0003 says its backup is encrypted and the key never goes into a backup.
- An off-site copy nobody on the project has to keep a machine running for. Today the only copy is on maderas.

HOW IT HAS TO BE TAKEN: ADR 0005 says nothing but the app may open the store, so a snapshot is a job inside the app during the night window (CHECKPOINT and copy, or EXPORT DATABASE), not a script reading the file from outside.

QUESTIONS FOR ANDONY / STAFF:
- Whose Drive: an OSU shared drive or a person's? Who can read it? A copy of the main store includes taxon-obscured true coordinates, and ADR 0003 says a copy handed outside the trusted circle must go through a redacting export.
- What is the backup for: disaster recovery only, or also something staff open? The legacy system uploaded workingOccurrences.csv to Google Drive (docs/reference-implementation.md), and staff may be relying on it. If so, they need a readable export, and that is a separate thing from a restorable backup.
- Retention: how many nightly copies, and for how long?

DESIGN QUESTIONS FOR US:
- Keep the pull (maderas takes the snapshot, then pushes it to Drive), or give the app a Drive credential and let it push? A pushing app holds a credential that a compromised app could use.
- Monitoring. check-backup-age.sh watches maderas's disk; a Drive target needs its own staleness check.
- A restore drill: restore a backup into a fresh store and open it before cutover, not after something has gone wrong.
notes:
ANSWERED (Andony, meeting 2026-09-11):
- Destination: the Google Drive that OSU and Master Melittology already use. Staff already have access to it, so a copy of the main store there does not leave the trusted circle. Encrypting the private store is still required (ADR 0003).
- Purpose: recovery ONLY. Staff will not open these files, so the format can be whatever restores most reliably (a DuckDB copy, or EXPORT DATABASE) rather than something readable.
- The export staff and reporting DO read is a separate thing: a data dump in the legacy system's format. It has its own bead, linked here.
Still open: how many copies to keep and for how long, whether maderas pulls or the app pushes, monitoring, and the restore drill. The legacy system already authorised Google Drive over OAuth with the drive.file scope (OBP-Server server/src/controllers/OAuthController.js). It is worth checking whether the same Drive and that same authorisation route carry over.
2026-10-03: the destination is the 'Bee Line' folder on an OSU SHARED drive (driveId 0AFBsKw8_fFsRUk9PVA; rainhead@gmail.com reads it, cannot write). GitHub #126 lists what must be arranged outside the code: a service account added to the folder as Content manager (OSU Workspace must allow an outside member, else an OSU-owned Cloud project), retention (proposed 14 nightlies + monthly for a year), a Cloud project + key as a Fly secret, and BEELINE_PRIVATE_DB_KEY kept off the server. Decided in the write-up, pending Peter's objection: the APP pushes (ADR 0005 puts the snapshot in-process anyway; maderas's token lapses 2026-12-01), via COPY FROM DATABASE (DuckDB 1.5.5) under drive.file scope. Nora may have enough Drive access to do the folder step; nobody tagged yet.
Peter, 2026-10-03: he is a member of the shared drive through a non-OSU account (read-only), so the drive admits outside addresses and the service account can be added like any member; the OSU-IT fallback is moot. Someone with manager rights still has to add it — not Peter.
