So the first open question above is decided — a manual flag blocks, like a blocking rule — at least in the form staff asked for it; whether a softer, non-blocking 'please look at this' flag is also wanted is still open.

What that means now that print runs exist (beeline-1kb.2, merged 2026-09-18):

- Printability is already 'a positive count and no blocking finding' (printable_sample, schema/140), read through sample_qc_finding (schema/130). A manual hold that lands in that roll-up as a blocking finding takes the sample out of printable_sample, so out of pending_print_sample, so out of the next freeze — no change to the freeze itself, and the collector's front page and the sample page show it with no new surface. qc_finding is a UNION of rule views, so the hold is one more arm reading an authored table, and it needs a qc_rule row (say 'staff_hold', blocking) for the severity join and the catalog copy (test pins qc_rule to the message catalog).
- This is the BEFORE-the-freeze half. The AFTER half is beeline-1kb.3 (pull a sample out of a prepared run). They should share one design: a held sample that is already frozen into an unprinted run is exactly a pull. Decide whether placing a hold on such a sample pulls it, refuses, or just warns the printer on the run page.
- A hold on a sample whose labels are already on paper blocks nothing (there is nothing left to print unless the count rises) and should probably say so rather than look effective.
- The note is for two readers: the collector, who may need to fix something, and the printer, who needs to know why it is not in the run. 'Hold, reason, by whom, when, lifted by whom, when' — an authored event per ADR 0007, as the open question on storage already leans, since a hold the blow-away erases would silently release the sample into the next run.
- Who may hold: admins, like the other staff tools, until per-atlas staff exist. Who lifts it: any admin; the collector fixing the record does not lift it by itself, because the rule views cannot know the doubt is answered.

Still the inverse of beeline-1kb.9 (waivers), and the two want one design: a waiver is staff saying a firing rule is fine, a hold is staff saying a silent record is not.

title: Impersonation: staff view the app as a volunteer
description: Peter, 2026-09-10 (prepping for the Andony meeting): staff need to see the app exactly as a given volunteer sees it — their QC home, their listings, their record pages — to help them over the phone and to check what a volunteer is being told. The mechanism already exists as delegation's acting-for switch (src/app/acting.ts, beeline-oyl): a cookie naming a person, re-read every request, under which 'mine' means that person everywhere. Impersonation is the same switch without a person_delegate grant, available to admins only. Differences to decide: (1) the chrome must say loudly whose view this is, as the delegation chrome does; (2) writes — a sample edit or correction saved while impersonating is authored by the admin, never the volunteer, which is already how delegation credits corrections; probably impersonation should be read-only, or at least each write should record the impersonation; (3) admin rights stay with the signed-in person but the admin surfaces (/people, /jobs, scope picker) should presumably hide while impersonating, so the view is faithful; (4) entry point is the person's page on /people, 'view as'; (5) every impersonation is worth a row in person_activity or the change log, since it is a staff member reading someone else's records deliberately. Related: beeline-oyl (delegation), beeline-7c1 (per-atlas staff roles).
notes: 2026-09-10: built on branch impersonation, PR open. Decisions taken (Peter agreed): read-only, admin flag off for the duration, each switch-on recorded in private.impersonation. Close when the PR merges.
close_reason: Merged in #57: staff view Beeline as a volunteer from the person's page; read-only, admin flag off for the duration, each switch-on recorded in private.impersonation.

title: occurrenceRemarks: a field for recording why a record is anomalous
description:
Andony raised this on gh-17 (2026-08-31), and nothing in the model carries it yet.

He is considering an occurrenceRemarks field to capture anomalies and clarify data issues — in the immediate term to annotate the duplicate field numbers being worked through (2025 first, then back through 2024). It is a standard Darwin Core term, so it also travels to Ecdysis and GBIF, which is presumably the point: a downstream reader of a duplicated or renumbered record can be told why.

Design question before schema: this is authored data about a record (CONTEXT.md, Data handling), so it belongs with corrections and staff overrides rather than beside the upstream projection — and Beeline already records WHO changed something and WHY through the authored-change log (ADR 0007). Whether occurrenceRemarks is a new column, a projection of that log at export time, or both is the thing to decide. Do not add a free-text column to sample or specimen without answering it.

Blocked in part on beeline-1kb.5: what the remarks would SAY about a duplicate depends on whether resolving one renumbers a specimen or not.

title: A staff coordinate override does not survive the nightly: promotion overwrites sample_location unconditionally
description:
Split out of beeline-ewl (Peter, 2026-08-30): the change LOG observes and never argues; whether a write should have happened is this bead's question, not the log's.

ingest/promote-observations.sql rewrites sample_location's coordinates, uncertainty and source unconditionally on every run, so a staff coordinate override survives until the next nightly and then vanishes. sample_location.source already carries 'staff_entry' in its CHECK vocabulary — written by nothing today; it is the intended hook.

Shape: ADR 0004's three-way merge, ported to location. A staff-entered location outranks inat_* and is never overwritten by promotion; upstream converging to the staff value retires the override; upstream moving to a third value leaves the override standing and surfaces a correction_conflict finding. Belongs with the staff override screen work that beeline-6e9 unblocked — the screen is the first writer of staff_entry.

Related decision deliberately NOT taken here: whether a materially different upstream coordinate on an already-printed sample should be flagged (count_below_printed's shape). That is a QC rule, later.
notes:
Changed in scope by the 2026-09-11 decision on beeline-1kb.2: once any specimen has been minted from an iNaturalist-backed sample, promotion takes no upstream edits to that sample except the host. So for minted samples, promotion must not overwrite sample_location at all, whether or not staff have overridden it. This bead's three-way merge still applies to samples that have not been minted yet, which is every sample until the first real print run.
CORRECTION (2026-09-14): my earlier note put the lock at minting and made it cover all of sample_location. Both are superseded (beeline-1kb.2):
- The lock starts when labels print, and covers date, locality and coordinates only.
- For printed samples, legacy-printed ones included, promotion must not overwrite the coordinates. Their uncertainty and source presumably hold with them, since those describe the same numbers.
This bead's three-way merge for staff overrides still applies to everything that is not held.

beeline-649 (2026-09-25) built the locality half of this shape: data/sample-overlay.csv keyed inat:<observation id>, applied as the sample_locality_override satellite at the end of observation promotion, with the follow rule excluding overridden samples and a diverged view instead of a QC finding. The coordinate override should take the same file (a second field) and the same applier; what differs is that a location is a pair plus uncertainty in sample_location rather than one text column.
close_reason: Merged as #99: coordinates are the second field of data/sample-overlay.csv, applied as sample_location_override with sample_location written beside as staff_entry; promotion's location upgrade skips overridden samples; observation_location is now a view.

title: A coordinate outside North America on a record that says it is inside
description:
New blocking QC rule qc_rule_coordinate_out_of_region: a sample_location outside 14..84 N, 172..50 W on a sample whose own country is USA/CAN/MEX or absent.

The signature is a pin moved after its place_guess was written. iNaturalist recomputes place_ids and leaves place_guess alone, so such an observation carries an Oregon locality string and an empty place list — an open-ocean point is inside no place. Nothing else notices: a sample's atlas comes from state_province, never from its point, so the record reads as well placed everywhere except the point itself.

Four rows on the dev store, all settled, none newly blocked (all four already block for other reasons): two sign-flipped longitudes (44.136, +120.701 and 44.6807, +121.1523 — central Oregon written as central Asia), one Portugal on a USA record, and sample 122269 at -7.08, -121.58 in the open Pacific. coordinate_uncertainty catches only the last, and only by luck: its observation carries an accuracy circle of 1,196 km. A sign-flip is as precise as any other pin.

The country clause is what keeps it from being the kind of finding that damages data (beeline-4dt): the fifth row outside the box is a record that says NZL and sits in New Zealand, which is honest and which no edit could satisfy, findings having no accepted state. The box is generous on purpose — the atlases' own footprint would flag 144 open-season locations that are members travelling.

Decided with Peter 2026-08-29: blocking rather than warning, since coordinates are exported and a printed specimen is permanent; box 14..84 N, 172..50 W.
close_reason: Landed as #30 (0a571e2). Blocking rule, box 14..84 N / 172..50 W with the USA/CAN/MEX-or-absent country clause. Four findings on the dev store, all settled: two sign-flipped longitudes, one Portugal coordinate on a USA record, and sample 122269 in the open Pacific. pending_print_sample unchanged.

title: elevation:fetch cannot run on maderas: rsync failure aborts before the GLO-30 fallback
description:
src/fetch-dem.ts rsyncs SRTM tiles from `beeline:` (the legacy production server) and only falls through to Copernicus GLO-30 for what that archive lacks. On maderas there is no `beeline` host in ~/.ssh/config, so rsync exits 255 — 'Could not resolve hostname beeline' — and rsyncFromLegacy throws before any GLO-30 fetch is attempted. The sandbox therefore cannot fetch a tile at all, and the nightly pipeline only derives: missingTiles is reported and the gap stays open forever.

Hit while bringing the sandbox up to date after minting (beeline-oyq): 786 minted samples left 32 elevation gaps behind n42_w115 and n43_w116. Worked around by curling both tiles from the GLO-30 bucket by hand into data/dem/ with the _glo30.tif suffix locateTile expects; derive then filled all 32.

Fix: treat an unreachable legacy archive the way a partial transfer is already treated — the re-check via absentTiles() already reports exactly what did not land, so an rsync that transfers nothing is not a different outcome from one that transfers some. Warn and continue to GLO-30 rather than throwing. (A genuinely broken rsync invocation would then surface as every tile coming from GLO-30, which is visible in the summary.)
notes: Fixed by PR #29 (branch dem-tiles-without-a-credential): the rsync is gone, SRTM now comes from OpenTopography's no-auth bucket and GLO-30 as before, both over HTTPS. Close this when that merges. Follow-up on whether the nightly should fetch its own tiles is filed separately.
close_reason: Fixed by #29 (3d77b82): SRTM now comes from OpenTopography's no-auth bucket and GLO-30 from Copernicus, both over HTTPS, so no host needs an ssh key or a forwarded agent to fetch a tile. A transport failure on the first source is reported and falls through instead of ending the run. Verified end to end on both 404 shapes and on 10 real tiles fetched to the dev checkout in 9.5s. Follow-ups: beeline-y2f (should the nightly fetch its own tiles) and beeline-hcz (neededTiles reads elevation_m IS NULL where derivation reads sample_elevation_pending).

title: observation_locality accepts 'Deschutes Co.' as a locality
description:
observation_locality (schema/108) refuses a county-only place_guess component —
the design says so, and 'Linn County, US-OR, US' is one of the refusals it
lists. But it only ever caught the LONG spelling, because the refusal came from
`county` being a word in the street-suffix list. The abbreviation walks
straight through: 'Deschutes Co.', 'Crook Co.', 'Lake Co', 'Wheeler Co'.

The component order makes it worse than a near-miss. The rule takes the FIRST
usable component, and these guesses put the county first, so the county WINS
over the town sitting right behind it:

  Deschutes Co., Bend, OR, US        -> 'Deschutes Co.', not 'Bend'
  Lake Co., Paisley, OR, US          -> 'Lake Co.',      not 'Paisley'
  Jefferson Co., Camp Sherman, ...   -> 'Jefferson Co.', not 'Camp Sherman'

MEASURED on the dev store (2026-08-29): 583 observations carry a county where
the next component is a real town name. A further 116 carry a bare county and
nothing else (21 of them open-season, all four-letter 'Chelan Co' spellings) —
those become no locality at all, which is the documented outcome for a guess
too coarse to use and the volunteer's to fix upstream on iNaturalist.

The county is already its own label field, so a locality that restates it
prints nothing and costs the label its only fine-grained place.

FIXED in beeline-4dt, because the anchor there took away the accident by which
`lane` was refusing 'Lane Co.' and something had to state the rule properly:
observation_locality's administrative clause now names the county beside the
state and the country, data-driven off observation_place.county_name, matching
'<county> County', '<county> Co' and '<county> Co.'.
close_reason: Landed in #27 (squashed as dd950f8).

title: One observation, several samples: sample.inat_observation_id is not unique and nothing names it
description:
Found while settling the reference question for beeline-ewl, by testing
whether inat_observation_id could key a sample change log. It cannot, and the
reason is its own defect.

sample.inat_observation_id has NO UNIQUE CONSTRAINT, and the data uses that:
150 observations are cited by two or more samples, 306 samples in total, worst
case four samples on one observation.

sample_multi_observation (schema/108) names the OPPOSITE case — one collecting
event iNaturalist records in several observations, which is expected and
explained. Nothing names this one, and it is not expected.

TWO SHAPES, both same-collector:

  120  same collector, same date, DIFFERENT sample numbers
       obs 129100300 -> samples 147 and 148, both 2022-07-31, same collector
       obs 163515852 -> samples 12 and 13, both 2023-05-21

   29  same collector, same number, DIFFERENT dates
       obs 201443458 -> sample 1 on 2021-07-29 and sample 1 on 2021-08-01
       obs 286091952 -> sample 7 on 2025-05-28 and sample 7 on 2025-06-01

    1  DIFFERENT collectors — the most suspicious of the lot, worth looking at
       first

ORIGIN IS THE LEGACY IMPORT, not minting. All 306 samples pre-date the minting
step (beeline-oyq): 0 were created by it, and minting cannot produce this —
it excludes an observation already named by some sample before grouping, and
free-links only samples citing no observation. The staging carries it
directly: 180 URL groups in legacy_occurrence share one observation URL across
more than one sampleID, so the Label Czar's records already had it and
promotion faithfully copied it through arg_min(p_inat_obs_id).

WHY IT MATTERS. Observation promotion keys on inat_observation_id, so both
samples receive the SAME believed-true coordinates, the same geoprivacy, the
same host taxon and the same elevation clearing — from one observation that
can only describe one of them. At least one of every pair is being given
another collecting event's location. qc_rule_count_mismatch likewise compares
both against the same observation's specimen count, so at least one is flagged
on evidence that is not about it.

It also quietly widens beeline-ewl: a change log keyed on the observation
would attach one history to two records.

NOT OBVIOUSLY A UNIQUE CONSTRAINT. Adding one would make legacy promotion fail
on real production data rather than describe it, and the right resolution
differs by shape — consecutive numbers on one day may be one collecting event
split in two, while the same number on two dates is two events sharing a
pasted URL. Name it first, in the sample_multi_observation idiom, and let the
count decide whether it is worth a curation pass before cutover.
close_reason: Fixed in #123: sample_shared_observation, with migration 0042

title: QC home's settled-samples link goes to everyone's flagged samples, not yours
description:
Peter, 2026-08-29, from his own dashboard: the QC home says

  "1 older sample of yours still carries a flag. Seasons settle on 1 March,
   so earlier ones no longer wait for you here - fixing them is welcome, not
   expected. Show them"

and "Show them" goes to EVERYONE's flagged samples. The count is his, the
destination is not.

CAUSE. listingHref (src/app/listings.ts) leaves defaults out of the URL so
that the plain path is the plain listing, and it treats MINE as the default:

  if (merged.scope !== MINE) params.set("scope", merged.scope);

But scope has no single default. MINE is the default for a VOLUNTEER, who
cannot reach anything else. For staff, parseListingQuery reads

  params.get("scope") ?? opts.preferred ?? MINE

where `preferred` is the beeline_scope cookie that remembers where they last
were (src/app/server.tsx). So an explicitly requested MINE is dropped from the
href, the cookie answers instead, and an admin who last browsed `all` gets
everybody's.

The QC home is the only caller that passes scope to listingHref, and the
comment directly above it asserts the property the function does not deliver -
"with the scope named, so a staff member's remembered scope does not answer
instead". The test asserted the same intent in prose and the bug in code:

  // Exactly what settling removed: this person's own, earlier seasons,
  // flagged - not every flagged sample, and not a remembered staff scope.
  expect(body).toContain(`href="/samples?season=settled&qc=flagged"`)

Only staff see it, and only staff who have used the scope switcher, which is
why it survived. The scope switcher itself is fine - it is a <select
name="scope"> in a GET form, so the value is always submitted.

FIX, written and tested, sitting on branch fix-mine-scope-in-listing-links
(not pushed as a PR: Peter, "we could leave this out of the pr, there will be
a lot of refinement work anyway"). One line - honour an explicitly named scope
even when it is the default:

  if (overrides.scope !== undefined || merged.scope !== MINE) ...

A caller that passes no scope keeps the old rule. Tests: the href
listingHref now builds, the round trip through parseListingQuery with a
`preferred` cookie of 'all' resolving to MINE, the same URL WITHOUT the scope
correctly resolving to 'all', and the qc-experience assertion corrected.

ONE KNOCK-ON, worth a look during the refinement work rather than deciding
here: server.tsx remembers an explicit choice, `if (admin &&
c.req.query("scope") !== undefined)`, so following this link now also SETS an
admin's scope cookie to mine. Consistent with the switcher and arguably right -
you asked for mine and it sticks - but it is a side effect of clicking a link
in a note rather than of choosing a scope, and a staffer who then hits
/samples from the nav lands in `mine` without having asked.
close_reason: Merged in PR #53: listingHref honours an explicitly named scope even when it is the default.

title: Wire inat:fetch-places into the nightly pipeline, and stop re-asking for dead place ids
description:
Nothing keeps inat_place current. It was filled once by hand on the dev store
and on the sandbox (2026-08-29, beeline-2yt), and a sync brings in observations
naming places the cache has never seen — so the gap reopens on its own and
nothing notices.

WHY IT MATTERS ONCE MINTING LANDS (beeline-oyq): observation_place is the only
route from an observation to a state and therefore to an atlas. An observation
whose places are uncached resolves to nothing, so a sample minted from it would
get no state, no atlas, and a place_unrecognised finding — for no reason except
that a fetch had not run.

THE FIX is one step in the nightly pipeline (src/app/jobs/registry.ts), between
sync and promote:

  sync -> fetch-places -> promote -> elevation

fetchPlaces() already takes a connection and is incremental against
inat_place_uncached, so the step is a call. Ordinarily it is a no-op or a
single request: 2,553 of 2,556 ids on the dev store were cached in one pass, and
the view only refills when a sync introduces a new place.

TWO THINGS TO GET RIGHT:

1. THE STEP MUST NOT FAIL THE PIPELINE. It is the only outbound dependency in
   the run other than the sync itself, and an unreachable places endpoint is
   not a reason to skip promotion — a store with a slightly stale cache is
   fine, a store that skipped promotion is not. Catch and report, the way the
   elevation step reports missing tiles rather than aborting.

2. THE THREE DEAD IDS. 117476, 59614 and 186423 are named by observations and
   no longer exist upstream: iNaturalist answers /v1/places/{id} for them with
   HTTP 200 and an empty results array, not a 404. So inat_place_uncached can
   never be empty, the fetcher spends one request per run re-asking, and
   nothing can use that view as a "cache is complete" check. 117476 alone is on
   4,127 observations — it was a curated area place around Burns, Oregon that
   somebody deleted.

   Worth recording what was asked for and not returned, so it is not asked
   again, and so "uncached" means "not yet tried" rather than "tried and gone".
   A small known-absent set the view subtracts. Costs nothing today (the
   observations affected still resolve through their other place ids — all
   4,133 still get a county, and 4,130 a state) but it is the difference
   between a view that can be asserted empty and one that cannot.
close_reason: Merged in PR #54: fetch-places is a non-fatal nightly step between sync and promote; inat_place_absent records ids iNat does not have and the uncached view subtracts them; migration 0026.

title: Ask Andony: attribution for records belonging to no member atlas
description:
docs/questions.md "Printing and mailing" Q7 and "Taxonomy across the atlases"
Q3 — the same question asked from two ends, and the one printing question the
walkthrough with Arthur cannot settle, because it is a program decision rather
than a bench practice. For Andony.

~2,660 specimens were collected where none of the six member atlases reaches,
by people who are either atlas members travelling or Master Melittologists
with no atlas at all (beeline-lcl; `atlas_region` says "known region, no atlas
covers it"). The store can say "no atlas" honestly. It has no answer for what
to PRINT.

1. Whose name goes on their labels, and on their Ecdysis/GBIF records — the
   program, or the atlas that happens to process them?
2. Does processing a sample through an atlas (the Arizona-through-Washington
   arrangement) make that atlas the attribution, or only the handler?
3. When two atlases disagree about a name, whose reaches Ecdysis and GBIF?
   Same shape: an attribution decision wearing taxonomy's clothes. The
   modelling half is beeline-0zb, which defers until a second opinion is
   actually being read; this asks who speaks for the record downstream.

Why it is a bead and not a line in the walkthrough: beeline-1kb.4 has to
render a collector/atlas line and cannot invent one, and beeline-2c3.11
already settled the on-screen half — with no atlas to act on behalf of, the
program acts as itself. Whether the same rule holds on a physical label and in
a GBIF record is exactly what has not been asked.
close_reason: Wrong premise, and the repo already answered it. A label has six fields (location, coordinates, date, collector, method, field number) and carries no atlas or program name — reference-implementation.md, off LabelsSubtaskHandler.js — so there is no slot for 'whose name'; the collector's name is on it because they collected it, and travelling outside an atlas does not change that. CONTEXT.md already states the handling case positively: assignment to an atlas FOR PROCESSING is an explicit administrative action, so Arizona-through-Washington is handling and is already named as such. Residue is an eventual Ecdysis/GBIF institutionCode, which follows physical custody (OSAC/WSDA) rather than membership, and there is no export to decide it for. Routing no-atlas records to a staff queue is real and is beeline-e85. Closed as gh-16.

title: Ask Andony: who is Jane Pope? (evidence says withdraw Gretchen's grant over her records)
description:
docs/questions.md "People and accounts" Q1, with evidence that has since
turned the default around. The question was "is Jane Pope a third member of
the Pederson household?" — asked because her 31 samples file under `pandg`.
On 2026-08-28 Gretchen Pederson was granted `acts_for` reach over Jane's
records (ingest/person-overlay.csv) on the assumption that they are.

NOTE ON SOURCES: some of the evidence below is contact detail from the legacy
register (data/legacy/usernames.csv, gitignored). Do not restate it in this
tracker, in a commit message, or in a GitHub issue — refer to it, as here.

MEASURED 2026-08-28 against the dev store and the legacy register, and every
piece of it points away from the household reading:

- The register carries Jane Pope as her own separate person, with her own
  username, her own contact details, and a mailing address in a different
  town from the Pedersons'. The Pedersons are three register rows sharing
  one household address: Gretchen, Pete, and Robert — whose row encodes in
  its username the sample-number hack that OccurrenceService.js hard-codes.
- She collects nowhere near them. Her 31 samples are Union (11), Morrow (7),
  Umatilla (7), Lincoln (4), Grant and Linn — north-eastern Oregon, and her
  register town is in that area. Gretchen's 1,146 are Deschutes/Lake/Crook/
  Grant/Wheeler, out of central Oregon.
- She never collects WITH them: all 31 of her samples are solo.
- In staging her 157 legacy rows split two ways: 83 carry NO userLogin and
  the synthetic id 9991026, and only 74 carry `pandg`/843723.

So the likeliest reading is a separate volunteer, some of whose records were
entered under the Pedersons' login — not household. If that is right, the
`acts_for` grant is reach over a stranger's records and should be withdrawn
(blank the value in ingest/person-overlay.csv; the row for Gretchen currently
reads `name:Robert Pederson;name:Jane Pope` and should drop back to Robert
alone).

TO ASK ANDONY: who is Jane Pope, and is there any relationship to the
Pedersons at all? Withdraw unless he says otherwise — the evidence no longer
supports the assumption the grant was written on.

title: Ask Andony: per-atlas policy on revealing taxon-obscured coordinates downstream
description:
docs/questions.md "Taxon geoprivacy" Q1 (downstream half), Q2 and Q3 — the
half of the geoprivacy question that is NOT settled. Marked a go-live blocker
in the doc, and beeline-1kb.7 (the model side) explicitly parks the legwork
here: "the regulatory legwork itself (asking each atlas) stays with staff."
Until now nothing tracked the asking.

Settled already, and NOT what this asks: a collector sees their own true
coordinates, and their own atlas's staff see them, in-app and in CSV exports
(Peter, 2026-08-23). That is a participant reading their own records.
beeline-1kb.1.1 asks the remaining in-app piece (cross-atlas staff reads).

OPEN, per atlas, and to be put to Andony as the person who can route it to the
six atlas coordinators:

1. May true coordinates of taxon-obscured records be REVEALED downstream — on
   printed labels, and in exports that leave the program (Ecdysis, GBIF)?
   Beeline retains both coordinate pairs, so either answer is implementable;
   what is open is permission, and it may differ per atlas.
2. What binds each atlas here — sensitive-species regulations, state
   natural-heritage data-sharing agreements, iNaturalist's own terms for
   obscured coordinates? An atlas that answers "yes" for a reason that does
   not hold in its state has not answered.
3. Until an atlas answers: do its taxon-obscured records stay unprintable
   (current behaviour), or print with the obscured coordinates? This one is
   answerable now and unblocks the interim.

Answers land in CONTEXT.md and drive beeline-1kb.7's per-atlas policy column.
An atlas that never answers is the case the safe default has to cover.
notes:
From the 2026-09-11 decisions: Beeline exports nothing automatically downstream. Staff download specimen data and upload what they choose. So an atlas's answer on revealing taxon-obscured coordinates will be carried out by its staff, by hand, at upload. Two consequences:
- The staff download has to make a taxon-obscured record obvious.
- The question may need putting to the people who upload (Caleb Lankford and Karen Wright for Washington, Lincoln Best for Oregon) as well as to Andony.
docs/questions.md 'Taxon geoprivacy' says so as of PR #58.

title: Unclaimed samples: a per-atlas screen for records from people we do not know
description:
Peter, 2026-08-28: "The staff for the appropriate atlas will need a screen
where they can see samples from unknown people."

An observation arriving from an iNaturalist user the store holds no
inat_account for is, today, nothing at all — no person, no sample, no QC
finding, nobody to show it to (beeline-oyq: nothing mints a sample from an
observation in the first place). 128 distinct observers are in that position
on the dev store, across 4,453 observations that carry a sampleId and a
specimen count.

Note what "unknown" means precisely: they are not anonymous. They have an
iNaturalist account — they made the observation — and the store simply has no
person bound to it. So the screen's job is identification, and the two actions
it needs are the two the overlay already spells:

  bind    this observer is somebody already here (the commonest case: a
          volunteer whose legacy records exist under a different login, or a
          household member)
  admit   this observer is a person the store has never seen — overlay
          `create` plus an `inat_user_id` binding, which is also what lets
          them sign in, since the approval gate is an account bound to a
          person

That makes this the same act as beeline-2c3.33 (admit a person from /people
rather than by hand-editing the curated overlay), arrived at from the other
end: there, staff know who they want to add; here, the records tell them
somebody is missing.

ROUTING. "The appropriate atlas" is answerable even when the person is not:
atlas assignment is geographic (CONTEXT.md — never by pipeline or iNat
project), and the observation carries coordinates. So the queue is scoped by
where the sample fell, via atlas_region, exactly as the listings' atlas scope
already is. Records falling where no member atlas reaches need an owner too —
that is the program itself (beeline-lcl), and it is the same "whose is this"
question printing has open (docs/questions.md, Printing 7).

Blocked on both:
- beeline-oyq — there is no sample to show until observations create one.
- per-atlas staff roles — staff is one global allowlist today, so "the staff
  for the appropriate atlas" cannot be expressed.

Open, worth deciding with staff rather than guessing:
- Does an unknown observer's sample exist in the model while unclaimed
  (belonging to a placeholder person), or stay staged outside it until
  somebody claims it? The first makes it countable and floggable; the second
  keeps person clean. The correction overlay and field numbering both assume a
  collector, which argues for staging.
- Does an unclaimed sample age? A record nobody claims for two seasons is
  either a lapsed volunteer or a stranger who found the project.
- Is there any auto-claim? A legacy person whose recordedBy name matches the
  observer's iNat display name is a candidate, and beeline-eft is the standing
  warning about acting on that kind of resemblance without a human.

title: Per-atlas staff roles: staff is one global allowlist today
description:
Three places in the codebase say "until a per-atlas staff role exists" and
nothing tracks building one:

  AGENTS.md (browsing)        scope is mine / one atlas / outside / all —
                              "staff being the admin allowlist until a
                              per-atlas role exists"
  schema/010_people_atlases.sql:126  who administers a program-only member is
                              deliberately not modelled, "until per-atlas
                              staff roles exist (beeline-lcl)"
  docs/questions.md:32        the geoprivacy blocker: "Beeline has no
                              per-atlas staff role today (staff is a global
                              allowlist, beeline-2c3.21), so the all-atlases
                              scope currently shows them"

Today person_admin is presence-is-the-grant with no scope at all: an admin
reaches /jobs, /people, /design and every atlas's records. That was right while
staff were six people who know each other (CONTEXT.md: a high-trust
environment, atlas-level roles stay minimal until a need appears).

Two needs have now appeared, which is why this is filed rather than left as a
comment:
- The geoprivacy blocker asks whether one atlas's staff may see another's true
  coordinates. That question cannot be IMPLEMENTED either way without a role
  that names an atlas, however Andony answers it.
- Unclaimed samples need routing to "the staff for the appropriate atlas"
  (Peter, 2026-08-28) — see the blocked bead.

Design notes, not decisions:
- person_membership already says where a person BELONGS; this is a different
  question (what they may DO, and over whose records), so it wants its own
  table rather than a column there — the same reasoning that split membership
  from administration in schema/010.
- Scope in the listings is already the vocabulary: mine / one atlas / outside
  / all. A role could simply decide which of those a person may select,
  rather than inventing a second vocabulary.
- Keep the global admin: somebody has to run /jobs and grant the roles.

title: Store the shredded observation projection
description: Materialise observation_current_fields as observation_field: the JSON shred is ~200 ms for 63k observations, almost all of it in the two correlated $.ofvs subqueries, and three QC rules read it — so qc_finding cost ~670 ms and the QC home, both listings, printability and every record page paid it once.
close_reason:
Built and committed (02d14b3).

observation_field (schema/060) is the materialisation; observation_current_fields (schema/105) stays the definition and is now also what the table is refreshed from and checked against. Three QC rules, ingest/promote-observations.sql and src/promote-observations.ts read the table.

Measured on the dev store (66k samples, 63k observations), before → after:
  qc_finding             466 → 205 ms
  one sample's findings  416 → 199 ms
  printable_sample       399 → 211 ms
Identical row counts on both sides (7,624 findings, 60,904 printable), so the rules say exactly what they said.

Refresh (src/refresh-observation-fields.ts) runs in two places, and they are not the same rule twice: inside the sync run's transaction, which is what makes 'loads and their shred agree' true at every commit boundary and lets the alarm view be a real alarm; and at the head of promotion, because db:reseed carries observation_load into a fresh schema and tells you to promote — and promotion writes believed-true coordinates onto samples from this table, so an empty one links nothing and reports it as a number. That hazard was found while building, not designed for.

observation_field_stale (schema/105) names the disagreement, same shape as sample_elevation_stale. A test proves it fires when loads move without a refresh, and that the rules go silent on an unrefreshed table — which is why nothing may read it unrefreshed.

Migration 0017 fills the table as it creates it. Verified against a store built from the previous schema: drift before was exactly the two new objects, after was none. Applied to a copy of the dev store it ran in 837 ms and left the alarm empty.

8 new tests (test/observation-field.test.ts); 385 pass, typecheck clean.

title: DuckDB's schema evolution is the weak spot, and cutover is when it starts to matter
description:
Peter, 2026-08-27, after a day that hit four distinct DuckDB DDL limitations:
"this is a strong mark against duckdb for production."

Recording the evidence while the examples are concrete, so the choice at
cutover is made from a list rather than from memory. **Not a proposal to
switch** — [ADR 0001](../docs/adr/0001-duckdb-first-with-portable-sql.md)
picked DuckDB deliberately and [ADR 0005](../docs/adr/0005-app-process-owns-the-store.md)
re-affirmed it at phase 4, both with Postgres named as the escape hatch. This
is the file that escape hatch would be argued from.

**What was hit in one day, all of it schema evolution:**

1. **No `ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT`.** Migrations 0012, 0013 and 0015 all
   add a column with a constraint on a fresh build and cannot add the
   constraint to a deployed store. Three of five migrations written today.
2. **No `DROP COLUMN` on a referenced table.** `person` is referenced by nine
   tables, so beeline-6bw has no migration at all — dropping the dependent
   views first does not help, nor does splitting across transactions. The
   answer is a full `db:reseed`.
3. **`db:migrate --check` cannot see either.** It compares tables and columns
   via `information_schema`, never constraints and never view bodies, so a
   deployed store missing a CHECK reports clean. The tool cannot verify the
   thing the engine cannot do.
4. **WAL replay after DDL can leave the file unopenable** (beeline-vyi,
   beeline-c1b) — hence the CHECKPOINT-after-DDL rule in the runbook. Fixed
   upstream but not in the pinned version.

**Why this is worse than it looks today, and better than it looks on paper.**

The blow-away era hides all of it: pre-cutover a bad schema is fixed by
rebuilding, so none of these cost anything. Every one of them is a cost that
*starts* at cutover, when the store becomes the only copy of minted field
numbers and rebuilding stops being free. So the era that makes DuckDB
comfortable ends exactly when its weakness begins — and the roadmap already
names December 2026 as that line.

Against switching, honestly: none of this touches what DuckDB was chosen for.
Reads are fast, the store is one file, there is no service to run or back up,
and the "lean on the database" principle is served by views that work fine.
The portable-SQL discipline has held — `schema/` is dialect-neutral by rule,
so the escape hatch is real rather than theoretical. And one dependency is
load-bearing and would need redesign: [ADR 0003](../docs/adr/0003-private-data-store.md)'s
private store is encrypted **as a whole file**, which Postgres has no
equivalent of; sessions and OAuth tokens would need a different protection
story.

**What would settle it:** whether anything else in the schema still has to
change after cutover. If the model is stable by December, these limits are
paid once and the file-shaped simplicity keeps winning. If phases 5–7
(printing, determinations, export) are still moving the schema in 2027, three
of the four above bite repeatedly and Postgres buys back more than it costs.
Worth revisiting when phase 5's schema lands, which is the first real test.
notes:
2026-08-27, after actually looking (Peter's framing: syntax is no cheaper to fix later; what matters is where DuckDB's capabilities shaped the design).

TWO SUPPOSED COUPLINGS DISSOLVE, and Peter is right about both:

- The private store becomes a *schema*, not a second database. Cross-schema joins are native in Postgres — better than DuckDB's ATTACH, not worse — so session.ts's 12 cross-boundary references and roster.ts's 2 stop being remarkable.
- Whole-file encryption loses its purpose rather than its implementation. ADR 0003's stated rationale is that 'the main database file is *meant* to be copied casually — backups, analytics, handing a snapshot to a student'. That is a DuckDB property. Postgres files do not travel; you hand over a dump, whose contents you choose. Role grants on a private schema plus pg_dump --exclude-schema are more granular than an encrypted blob you can either open or not.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DEEP, in order:

1. NO INDEXES ANYWHERE. schema/*.sql declares not one CREATE INDEX. Every lookup in the app is a full scan over 380,279 specimens and 256,161 determinations, and DuckDB is fine with that because it is columnar and vectorised. Postgres is not. Every FK and every filter column would need one, and the 'rules are views' design — QC rules, printability, determination-of-record — is a stack of views over those scans. Mechanical once you know which indexes; the risk is the views written in shapes no index helps (the locality regex rules). This is the coupling that bites silently and late, and nobody has had to think about access paths once.

2. ADR 0005's embedded single-writer model. 48 DuckDBInstance/connect sites, the file lock that makes 'one process owns the store' true, stop-the-service-to-migrate, in-process jobs under interactivity SLAs with a night carve-out. Postgres inverts all of it — and much of it stops being *necessary*, which is a gain, but the operational design and the whole deploy runbook are written against embedding.

3. 1,464 lines of ingest SQL where tables materialise from files: read_csv x6 across seed-animals/promote-determinations/promote-legacy, read_ndjson for the 383k-row legacy load. Postgres wants COPY FROM STDIN streamed from the client, or parsing in TS. ADR 0001 explicitly exempts this layer, so nothing has protected it and nothing was meant to — but it is the layer that keeps growing.

The app itself reads no files through the engine at request time: applyPersonOverlay takes parsed rows, corrections.ts uses none. That boundary is clean.

So the ranking is roughly the reverse of the syntax finding: the schema ports in a day, the *absence of indexes* is the thing that would decide whether the design survives the move at all.
Second instance of "no DROP COLUMN on a referenced table", 2026-08-28.

beeline-6bw removed person.pronouns from schema/*.sql (9334a17). A store built
before that commit still has the column, and it cannot be removed:

  $ duckdb b.duckdb -c "ALTER TABLE person DROP COLUMN pronouns"
  Dependency Error: Cannot alter entry "person" because there are entries that
  depend on it.

Found by db:migrate's own drift check while migrating a dev-store copy to head
for beeline-oyl. The remedy is db:reseed (beeline-j4r) — there is no migration
to write, because writing one means rebuilding person and restating every view
that depends on it, which is the derived layer copied out of schema/*.sql.

The point for this bead: the cost was zero, and the reason it was zero is that
reseeding is still free. The same column after cutover would be permanent —
not because it holds anything, but because the store would by then be the only
copy of the field numbers and could not be re-derived from staging.

title: Remove pronouns from the model entirely
description:
Decided 2026-08-27 (Peter): drop pronouns from the system. They are sensitive
and unnecessary — anyone who wants to state theirs can do so in a free-text
profile page.

Supersedes [beeline-0qr](../.beads/), which was the open design question about
vocabulary, multiple sets, and how the closed list would translate across
English, Spanish and Canadian French. That question dissolves rather than gets
answered: the reason it was hard is the reason not to hold the data.

The surface to remove:

- `schema/010_people_atlases.sql` — the `pronouns TEXT CHECK (pronouns IN
  ('he','she','they'))` column, its `COMMENT ON COLUMN`, and the clause in the
  `person` table comment that says name parts and pronouns "sit here together
  because all of them answer 'how to refer to this person'".
- A migration. DuckDB has no `DROP COLUMN` restriction here, but check —
  and note the deployed store currently holds the column with, as far as
  anyone knows, no rows filled.
- `src/model.ts` — the `Pronouns` type and `person.pronouns`.
- `src/app/messages/en.ts` — the `pronounForms` block (subject/object/
  possessive per set), which exists only to render the stored value.
- `src/app/views/design/voice.tsx` — the guidance paragraph and the
  "Don't guess pronouns" line. Some of what that page says is still true and
  worth keeping in a form that does not reference a stored field: never infer
  how to refer to someone from their name, and write neutrally by default.
- `test/messages.test.ts` ("has all three pronoun sets the schema allows"),
  `test/schema.test.ts` ("pronouns accept the starting vocabulary and reject
  the rest"), and whatever `test/person-overlay.test.ts` asserts.
- Check whether the person overlay can set the field before removing, since
  a curated CSV row naming a dropped field must not start failing silently.
- `docs/adr/0005` mentions the pronoun vocabulary as an example of a decision
  deferred to the message catalog; that reference should go or be re-pointed.

Two things to decide while doing it, neither of which should hold up the
removal:

1. **The free-text profile page does not exist.** A column with no screen to
   fill it is worse than no column, so this bead removes and does not replace;
   the profile page is its own piece of work when someone wants it.
2. **The store already holds `person.display_name` and name parts**, which is
   all the app needs to refer to anyone. Nothing else read `pronouns` — the
   catalog block was speculative, written before any screen used it, which is
   the clearest sign it was not load-bearing.
close_reason: person.pronouns, the Pronouns type, the catalog's pronounForms block, and the /design/voice guidance that referenced a stored field are all gone; three tests removed and one reworded. /design/voice keeps what is still true: never infer how to refer to someone from their name, write neutrally, and neutral is the whole rule rather than a fallback. No migration is possible — DuckDB refuses DROP COLUMN on person because nine tables reference it — so the column goes at the next db:reseed, which ADR 0006 and the runbook now name as the answer for changes migrations cannot carry. 361 tests pass.

title: No page for one specimen: the determination history is modelled and unreadable
description:
There is no route for a single specimen or a single sample. `/samples` and
`/specimens` are the only read surfaces, `/samples/:id/edit` is a five-field
form for non-iNat place data, and `/people/:id` is the only detail page in the
app.

`determination` is append-only and `determination_of_record` is a view: a
correction is a newer event, never an edit, and an expert never overwrites a
volunteer. That is the right model and the app has no way to look at it. The
specimens listing gives a determination one cell, which shows the record and
nothing else — not that an expert overrode a volunteer, not when, not through
which channel, not what the volunteer had said. `determination.verbatim_
identification` reaches the specimen CSV and no screen at all
([beeline-tgu](../.beads/)).

This is the Symbiota mirror-image. Their bug is a rich `omoccurdeterminations`
alongside a flattened copy on the occurrence that drifts from it; the
archaeology's advice is to model assertions and not the flattened copy
(https://gist.github.com/rainhead/7428e51bcbfc98108e191a7ec476a062, lesson 2).
We did that and then built only the flattened read.

**What the page holds.** One specimen: field number, its sample, and the
determination history in `recorded_at` order — who, when, which channel,
expert or not, the qualifier, the verbatim name, and which row is the record.
From the sample: collectors in order, dates, place, coordinates with their
`source` provenance and geoprivacy beside them, elevation with its
`elevation_source`, and the sample's QC findings.

**Why it is worth building before its phase.** Two things already queued need
somewhere to live and would otherwise each invent it:

- Phase 6's "add a determination" is an action on a specimen, and the page is
  where a determiner sees what has already been said before saying anything.
- Phase 5's proofing pull ("what causes Arthur to pull a record out of a run",
  beeline-1kb.1) is a question about one record, and "why is this not
  printable" has no answer surface today.

Gating and scope follow the listings exactly: `mine` is forced for volunteers
and follows the acting-for switch (`src/app/acting.ts`), so reaching a
specimen is reaching its sample. A URL for one record is also the thing a
volunteer pastes into an email about it, which nothing in the app currently
gives them.

Open: whether the sample gets its own page too or the specimen page carries
the sample inline. A sample with 2,252 specimens (the largest trap sample)
argues for a sample page with a specimen list; a net sample with three argues
against the extra hop.
close_reason:
Both pages built (the open question answered as 'both', Peter, 2026-08-27).

/specimens/:id: the determination history as events — who, when, which channel, expert or not, the qualifier, verbatim_identification, sex/caste, notes — newest first, with determination_of_record MARKED rather than hoisted, since hoisting it rebuilds the flattened read. Where the record is not the newest the page says why; that is 61,102 specimens on the dev store, so it is the common case rather than an edge.

/samples/:id: the sample in full — collectors in order, dates, method and protocol, place, atlas (with 'no atlas' as an answer), floral host (row absent, not blank, when there was no flower), the observation — plus coordinates with their source provenance and the observation's geoprivacy beside them, elevation with its elevation_source and a stale note, the QC findings in the same words the QC home uses, and a paged list of its specimens. QC findings are sample-keyed, which is why the sample got its own page: on a 2,252-specimen trap sample they would otherwise have been reachable only through one arbitrary specimen. It also gives /samples/:id/edit the parent it never had.

Both pages carry the whole of the other's sample block through shared components (SampleFacts / WhereCollected / SampleFlags), so the two cannot drift into two accounts of one sample.

Gating follows the listings with the filters gone: volunteer reaches their own, staff reach everything, mine follows the acting-for switch, and unreachable answers 404 rather than 403 so a URL cannot be probed. Linked in from both listings and the QC home.

Also: DetailList (new component, proofed at /design/components + CSS), and place/dateRange hoisted into the catalog's formatters where three views had retyped them.

Committed 9266108. 16 new tests in test/record.test.ts; 377 pass, typecheck clean.

Follow-up: beeline-2c3.35 (a record page costs a full qc_finding scan).

title: Build a corpus of real verbatim strings and test every parser against it
description:
We turn verbatim text into structure in more places than we test, and every one
of them is a lexical guess against data we have but have never surveyed. The
guesses are cheap to make and expensive to discover wrong — a mis-parsed
authorship or a mis-split name reaches a printed label, Ecdysis, and GBIF
looking exactly as settled as a correct one.

**Inventory of parse sites** (to be completed as part of this work — this is
what a grep found, not a proof):

- `ingest/seed-animals.sql:117` — authorship as "whatever follows the binomial":
  `regexp_replace(sci, '^[A-Za-z]+( \([A-Za-z]+\))? [a-z-]+', '')`. Assumes a
  hyphen is the only non-letter in an epithet, one capitalised genus token, and
  no hybrid marker.
- `ingest/seed-animals.sql:33,35` — genus and subgenus out of a `genus` column
  that sometimes holds `Lasioglossum (Dialictus)`; `[A-Za-z]+` only.
- `ingest/promote-legacy.sql:309` — `recordedBy` split on `|`, the collector
  list. This one is load-bearing for attribution and for "my samples".
- `ingest/promote-legacy.sql:261` — identity fold to `[a-z0-9]`. Deliberate and
  already reasoned about, but it is a parser and belongs in the corpus.
- `ingest/promote-legacy.sql:164` — iNat observation id off the end of a URL.
- `src/person-name.ts` — `labelName()` deriving "P. Abrahamsen" from name parts,
  and whatever splits full names into parts upstream of it.
- Dates: legacy `day`/`month` (Roman numerals) / `year` / `verbatimEventDate`.

**What to build**

1. Harvest the real distinct verbatim strings from production staging for each
   site — every distinct `scientificName`, every distinct `recordedBy`, every
   distinct `identifiedBy`, every distinct `verbatimEventDate` — with counts.
   Land the *survey* (distincts + counts + what the current parser does with
   each) as a queryable view or a checked-in report, not a one-off query.
2. Promote the interesting tail into `test/fixtures/` and assert against it. The
   existing fixtures are synthetic (`legacy-occurrences.jsonl` is Ada Collector
   and Bea Trapper) and `test/promote-legacy.test.ts` makes exactly one
   authorship assertion. Real strings are the point.
3. Anything the parser gets wrong becomes either a fix or a curated-worklist row
   — `legacy_taxon_uncurated` and `legacy_determiner_unresolved` are already the
   right shape for "the parser declined, a human decides".

**Why now.** Phase 7 (Ecdysis/GBIF import) brings strings from outside our own
data entry, and phase 8 freezes Mongo — after which the corpus is the only
record of what the source actually said.

**What Symbiota's history predicts we will find**
(https://gist.github.com/rainhead/7428e51bcbfc98108e191a7ec476a062). Their
`parseScientificName()` is 120+ lines of accreted heuristics, copied into five
places, and in 9,287 commits over 16 years it is the *only* function that ever
earned a unit test — the gist's reading is that the function you finally test is
where the domain is genuinely hard. What it accumulated, each item from a real
bug: non-breaking spaces in both UTF-8 and Latin-1 (names pasted from Wikipedia
through Excel, still arriving in 2026); underscores from data exports; `?` and
`*`; `cf.`/`c.f.`/`cfr.`/`aff.`; `sp.`/`spp.` as a rank signal; hybrid markers as
ASCII `x` vs `×` (U+00D7) vs `×` glued to the genus; the extinction dagger `†`;
parenthesised subgenera; cultivar epithets parsed as authorship.

And the deepest one: to decide whether the second token is a specific epithet or
the start of an author string, it *queries the taxa table*. There is no purely
lexical answer. We are already better placed than they were — we parse once, at
ingest, against a curated list, with a worklist for the residue — but the same
fact holds, and the corpus is how we find out where.

Their matcher failure mode is worth designing against too: a duplicate detector
split "B. & C. Durden" on `&` and matched the token `B.` to "Lois B. O'Brien"
and "B. Daniel". We have the same scar (one stray name on one row collecting
1,675 samples). Tune toward precision — a curator trusts a tool that
under-reports far longer than one that over-reports.
close_reason: ingest/parse-names.sql is now the one place a verbatim name comes apart, with legacy_name_parse as the survey over every distinct string and legacy_verbatim_shape over the other parsed fields. Running it found two wrong rules and fixed both: authorship was taking a trinomial's third epithet (Osmia montana authored 'montana', Bembix americana 'spinolae', Colletes consors 'pascoensis' — and authorship prints on labels), and subspecies were recognised from taxonRank, which calls two of the five trinomials a species. Verified on production staging: 156 authorships and none an epithet (was 157 with 3 bad), 5 subspecies nodes (was 3), 0 unresolved determinations (was 1). test/legacy-name-parse.test.ts runs the real parser over strings lifted from that staging, near-exhaustively by category. legacy_name_flattened names what the model still cannot say: 25 morphospecies (beeline-8g7) and one 'nr.' (beeline-tgu). Other parsers surveyed clean: recordedBy uses '|' and nothing else, Roman-numeral months already handled, URL taxon-page rows correctly yield nothing.

title: A derived elevation does not record the coordinates it was derived from
description:
`sample_location.elevation_m` is, by its own COMMENT, "a property of these
believed-true coordinates, derived from them". Nothing in the store ties it to
*which* coordinates. If the latitude/longitude change, the elevation is silently
about a different place, and `src/derive-elevation.ts:97` will never revisit it
because it only ever selects `WHERE elevation_m IS NULL`.

Today exactly one write path remembers this. `ingest/promote-observations.sql:54`
nulls both `elevation_m` and `elevation_source_id` when the incoming coordinates
differ from the stored ones by more than 5e-5, which hands the row back to the
derive job. That is correct, and it is the only place the rule exists.

The other coordinate write paths do not have it, or do not exist yet:

- `source = 'staff_entry'` is already in the `sample_location.source` CHECK with
  no writer behind it; `/samples/:id/edit` does not touch coordinates today, and
  will.
- Legacy re-promotion is a second path.
- docs/roadmap.md phase 3 says "phase-3 sync can upgrade [legacy coordinates]" —
  a deliberate coordinate move on rows that already carry a legacy-derived
  elevation.
- Corrections (ADR 0004) are a fourth.

A wrong elevation here is printed on a physical label and is permanent
(CONTEXT.md), so this is the same class of hazard as beeline-6vc — that one is
about deriving an elevation the coordinate does not support, this one is about
keeping an elevation the coordinate no longer supports.

Fix in our idiom: make it an invariant the store can check rather than a
discipline every writer must remember. Options, cheapest first:

1. Store the coordinates the elevation was derived from (`elevation_lat`,
   `elevation_lon`, or a single hash column) and add a QC view that flags drift.
   Costs two columns; makes the question answerable by anyone, forever.
2. Keep the current null-on-move rule and add a test that enumerates every
   statement writing `sample_location.latitude` and asserts each one also clears
   elevation. Cheaper now, but it is a grep-shaped test that a new write path
   will quietly fall outside of.

Option 1 also makes a re-derivation against a different DEM tile
distinguishable, which `elevation_source.file_hash` was already built for.

Origin: the Symbiota archaeology gist
(https://gist.github.com/rainhead/7428e51bcbfc98108e191a7ec476a062), whose
sharpest recurring shape is that any new way to create or modify a record is a
new way to forget to re-index it — their `tidInterpreted` generated that bug
class for a decade.
close_reason: sample_location.elevation_latitude/longitude added (CHECK-paired with elevation_m); schema/170 states the staleness rule once as sample_elevation_stale + sample_elevation_pending; derive-elevation reads the pending view so a forgotten clear self-heals; promote-observations drops its duplicate tolerance in favour of the view; migration 0012 backfills. Verified on a copy of the dev store: 66,291 elevations backfilled with provenance, 0 stale. Tests: a moved coordinate re-derives with nobody clearing it, a rounding-level nudge does not, and promotion leaves nothing stale.

title: Determinations cannot record cf./aff./sp. — the glossary teaches qualifiers the store has no column for
description:
A determination carries `animal_id NOT NULL` and nothing else about *how sure*
the determiner was. There is no `identification_qualifier` and no
`verbatim_identification` (schema/040_determinations.sql).

Meanwhile the rest of the system behaves as though qualifiers exist:

- `TaxonName` (src/app/views/components/taxon.tsx) takes a `qualifier` prop and
  places it by rank; `/design/names` demos `cf.`, `aff.`, `sp.`, `spp.`,
  `s. str.`
- The volunteer glossary defines them as things a volunteer will encounter —
  `cf-aff` (src/app/messages/en.ts, "cf. means the specimen resembles that
  species and needs confirming; aff. means it is close to it but probably
  something else") and `sp` ("sp. means one unnamed species in that genus").

So today a determiner who means *cf. Bombus occidentalis* must either assert
the species flatly — overclaiming, and on a printed label that is permanent —
or drop to genus, which throws away the resemblance they actually observed.
Neither is what they know. Every determination we hold is a bare positive
assertion.

`sp.`/`spp.` are arguably already expressible (a determination at genus rank
*is* "genus known, species not"), so the render can derive them. `cf.` and
`aff.` cannot be: they modify a species-rank assertion and no rank stands in
for them.

Second half of the same gap: `verbatim_identification`. Legacy promotion
resolves the verbatim `scientificName` to the deepest matching `animal` node
and keeps no copy of the string. That is survivable while Mongo staging is
re-pullable; it stops being survivable at cutover, and `channel =
'ecdysis_import'` (phase 7) will bring back both verbatim names and qualifiers
from a system that does record them.

Scope to decide:
- `determination.qualifier TEXT CHECK (qualifier IN ('cf.', 'aff.'))` — or a
  wider vocabulary if the determiners use one. Ask at beeline-r33 (expert
  determination discovery) rather than guessing.
- `determination.verbatim_identification TEXT` for imported channels.
- Whether printability treats a qualified determination as printable, and what
  the label prints.

Origin: reading the Symbiota archaeology gist against our schema
(https://gist.github.com/rainhead/7428e51bcbfc98108e191a7ec476a062). Symbiota's
`omoccurdeterminations` carries `verbatimIdentification`,
`identificationQualifier`, `identificationVerificationStatus`; the gist's
lesson is that a schema representing only positive assertions cannot express
what taxonomists actually know — morphospecies, illegitimate names, `cf.`,
`aff.`, excluded species.
close_reason: determination.qualifier (cf./aff./nr., CHECK-constrained) and determination.verbatim_identification added; migration 0013; determination_of_record carries both. sp./spp. deliberately omitted — a genus-rank determination already means that. Legacy promotion resolves 'Lasioglossum nr. tenax' (3 records) to the species node with qualifier nr. instead of the bare genus, and keeps the verbatim string on every expert determination that had one (30,492 of 187,011 — the rest arrive already parted, so none is invented). nr. joins cf. and aff. in TaxonName, /design/names and the glossary; the qualifier travels through both listings and their CSVs. Vocabulary is the three open-nomenclature qualifiers that modify a species assertion; if determiners use others, beeline-r33's discovery is where that arrives.

title: Admit a person who has no records: the overlay 'create' field
description: Promotion only ever mints people from records, so a staff member who never collects — an intern, a coordinator — could not be in the store at all, and therefore could not sign in (the approval gate is an inat_account row). Nora Jacobi (njacobi, 10206031) is the first: no legacy records, no observations. Adds a 'create' overlay field asserting that a person exists, applied before every other row so account binding and admin grant compose with it. Replayable like every other decision, which a hand-written INSERT would not be — db:reseed rebuilds person from staging.
close_reason: Closed

title: Sign-in returns you to the page you asked for
description: The session gate refused a GET and offered a sign-in button that always landed you on the home page, so a link into a sample, a filtered listing, or a person's page cost you the page you came for. The gate now hangs the requested path on the sign-in link, /auth/inat stores it in a short-lived cookie beside the OAuth state, and the callback redirects there. Same-site paths only (no absolute, scheme-relative, or backslash URLs; no /auth/ loop), and GETs only, since a POST cannot be replayed after the detour through iNaturalist.
close_reason: Closed

title: Curate the 25 people the legacy name register disagrees with
description:
The register (beeline-8t8) is fetched and staged, and `legacy_register_name_conflict` reports 45 rows across 25 people on the real store. Nothing writes any of them to `person`: deciding is a human job, and the verdicts go in `ingest/person-overlay.csv` like every other name decision.

What the 25 break down into, measured 2026-08-25:

FIVE FAMILY NAMES, where the register is probably right and promotion cannot see it:
  Hailey Balock -> Blalock          (the store's spelling looks like a transposition)
  Melissa Dusoleil -> DuSoleil      (capitalisation inside the name)
  Betsy Lane -> Lancefield Lane     (a fuller family name; changes the label)
  Madeline Herrmann -> Hermann      (which of the two is right is not obvious)
  Tom Robertson -> Biddle           (NOT a correction: tom_julie is a shared
                                     household login and the register row is
                                     Julie Biddle's — beeline-oyl)

FOURTEEN GIVEN NAMES, nearly all a nickname against a formal name, in both
directions: Kim/Kimberly, Cort/Corey, Nate/Nathaniel, Judi/Judith,
Cindy/Cynthia, Phil/Philip, Marty/Martin, Rick/Richard, but also
William/Bill and Emily/Emma Hoskins (already curated in
ingest/collector-aliases.csv by beeline-eyk). These are not errors either
way — they are a question about what each person calls themselves, and the
store's answer comes from the spelling they last recorded under.
Also: MaryJo -> Mary Jo, which the register has right, and which
src/person-name.ts already cites as its worked example.

THREE LABEL INITIALS the register holds and derivation cannot produce:
  Juan Manuel Benitez Alvarez -> 'J.M.'  (genuine: person.label_name)
  Arndt Arndt -> 'J.'                    (a register row whose firstName holds
  Heather Davis -> 'H.'                   the surname — but 'J.' says the real
                                          given name starts with J)

Suggested order: the five family names first (they change what a label
prints), then the three initials, then the nicknames last or never — asking
the person is better than picking for them, and the volunteer-facing app
will eventually let them say.
notes:
CORRECTION (2026-08-25, after Peter asked whether 'Lancefield Lane' was a
street): the five family names were written up as 'the register is probably
right'. Checked against each person's iNat login and profile name, ZERO of the
five are confirmed corrections, and one runs the other way.

The login is the cheap adjudicator, and it was there all along:

  Madeline Herrmann -> 'Hermann'   REGISTER IS WRONG. Login 'mherrmann', iNat
                                   profile 'Mady Herrmann', signs Herrmann on
                                   115 records. Three independent corroborations
                                   of the store. (Also: she goes by Mady.)
  Tom Robertson -> 'Biddle'        Not a name question. 'tom_julie' carries BOTH
                                   spellings across 4056 records — the household
                                   login of beeline-oyl.
  Betsy Lane -> 'Lancefield Lane'  REAL, not a street: her login is
                                   'blancefield', and 'Lancefield' appears
                                   nowhere in her address column. A maiden name.
                                   But she signs 'Betsy Lane' on all 37 of her
                                   records, so this is hers to choose, not ours
                                   to correct.
  Melissa Dusoleil -> 'DuSoleil'   Plausible casing fix. Login
                                   'melissadusoleil' is lowercase and cannot
                                   adjudicate; 14 records, all 'Dusoleil'.
  Hailey Balock -> 'Blalock'       UNRESOLVED. Login 'hailey_bird', iNat profile
                                   just 'Hailey', signs 'Balock' 47 times.
                                   Nothing in the store can settle it.

So the ordering advice below is wrong too. Better order: check each name
against the login and the iNat profile first — that resolves some for free and
costs nothing — and treat everything left as a question for the person rather
than a correction to apply. The register earns its place by RAISING these, not
by answering them.
close_reason: Superseded 2026-08-28: names are fixed on /people/:id by staff, not graduated into ingest/person-overlay.csv row by row. legacy_register_name_conflict stays as a report — 'what does the register think about this person' is worth being able to ask — but curating its 41 rows across 30 people is not a task anybody needs to sit down with. Emma/Emily Hoskins, the one with a decision attached, was settled separately (usernames.csv is the name of record).

title: The observer is not always the collector: no way to say so on an iNat-backed sample
description:
Raised by Peter, 2026-08-24: is there a way to override the collector for new
iNaturalist samples? There is not, at three levels.

1. Nothing creates a sample from an observation at all. promote-legacy.sql is
the only INSERT INTO sample in the codebase; sync LINKS observations to
samples that already exist, matching sample.inat_observation_id, which the
legacy rows carried. Creating a sample from an observation with no legacy row
is unbuilt, so post-cutover this is the path everything arrives by.

2. The arrow points the other way today. promote-observations.sql says "the
observer of a sample's evidencing observation is its collector", but uses it
to infer the ACCOUNT from sample.collector_id (set by legacy promotion from
recordedBy) and write inat_account. The observer never sets the collector, so
there is no place an override would attach.

3. In-app editing is closed to iNat-backed samples by construction:
src/app/sample-edit.ts filters WHERE inat_observation_id IS NULL. recordedBy
is not in the correctable vocabulary either, so ADR 0004 cannot do it for
legacy rows.

WHY IT MATTERS. beeline-2c3.20 set the principle: "in-app editing is for facts
iNaturalist cannot express, not for facts it owns." iNaturalist has exactly
one observer per observation, and the store already holds two populations
where the observer is demonstrably not the collector:

  - records somebody else typed in — Emily Carlson's 254 carry
    amelathopoulos because Andony entered them
  - shared household logins — both Pedersons collect under pandg (beeline-oyl)

So "who collected this" is a fact iNaturalist cannot express, and by the
stated principle it belongs in-app. Inheriting the observer silently is how
254 samples end up attributed to the person who did the typing.

WORTH DOING WITH beeline-2c3.20, not separately: same sample, same form, same
gate, and the same argument about what in-app editing is for. Deciding
co-collectors without deciding the primary leaves the more consequential half
inherited by default — the primary is who the sample number belongs to and
whose name prints first on the label.

Blocked on nothing technically; blocked in practice on the sample-creation
path existing, and on Andony's answers about households (docs/questions.md,
People and accounts).
notes:
beeline-oyl's design (decided 2026-08-25) leans on this bead. oyl keeps
inat_account 1:1 and adds a "may act for" delegation link for visibility; the
remedy for an individual sample attributed to the wrong collector is the
reassignment this bead describes, done together with beeline-2c3.20 as this
bead already argues.

Peter's framing, 2026-08-25: one primary and zero or more secondary collectors,
reassignable — including to a collector who has no account. The model already
has that grain (sample_collector, ordered, position 1 = sample.collector_id);
what is missing is any way to change it.

Two constraints from measuring the real data on 2026-08-25:

• THE PRIMARY IS NOT STABLE WITHIN A PAIR. sample_collector holds "Michael
  O'Loughlin + Dan O'Loughlin" on 312 samples and "Dan O'Loughlin + Michael
  O'Loughlin" on 23. Nothing may assume one member of a household or a regular
  pair is always the primary.
• REASSIGNMENT IS A CREDIT TRANSFER once Master Melittology progress ties to a
  person (oyl). Giving credit away is safe; claiming it is not. Suggested rule:
  the sample's current primary may reassign, and staff may; nobody may add
  themselves to a sample they are not already on.

Also relevant: the account-less collector is the normal case, not an edge one —
155 of 565 people have no inat_account and 145 of them are already the PRIMARY
collector on samples. A person picker for reassignment must reach them, and
must be able to mint a new one (beeline-wn2 is the control).

title: Support people and specimens from outside any member atlas
description:
Peter (2026-08-24): the model assumes everyone and everything belongs to one of the six member atlases. Neither is true, and the gap is already sized.

SPECIMENS. 632 samples carry no atlas_id, holding 2,664 specimens, collected by 44 people. They are real Master Melittologist records, not errors — NV 262, KS 67, AZ 66, MT 57, CA 46, YT 48 (split across country codes 'CA' and 'CAN', which is its own small bug), NY 18, CO 15, TX 13, WY 9, PA 9. iNat project 99706 exists precisely for these: it is the 'outside of Oregon' MM project.

PEOPLE. 186 of 584 have no home atlas after the usernames.csv load. 123 did not match the roster at all; 63 matched but gave a state no atlas covers (MT, CA, YT, KS, PA, NY, CO, AK) or left it blank. Separately, 11 people have samples of which NONE carry an atlas — they collect entirely outside the six.

The core problem is that absence means two different things. person_home_atlas has no row for 'we have not asked yet' AND for 'no atlas applies', and sample.atlas_id is NULL for 'outside the atlases' AND for 'geography did not resolve'. Those want telling apart before anyone counts on either — a dashboard that says '186 unknown' is useless if half of them are known to be outside.

Also unresolved by the current shape:
• The brand model gives a volunteer their atlas's colorway (beeline-2c3.11). What does an outside-any-atlas volunteer see? The program identity is the honest answer, which the model already supports — MM acts on behalf of an atlas, so with no atlas it just acts as itself.
• Listings scope is mine / one atlas / all atlases. There is no way to ask for 'outside the atlases', so those 632 samples are reachable only via 'all'.
• Exports and labels presumably want the program, not a member atlas, as the attribution.

Worth deciding before atlas branding and before anyone builds per-atlas reporting. Relates to beeline-fie (the load that surfaced this), beeline-2c3.11 (branding), and the staff-scoping decision.
notes:
Domain correction (Peter, 2026-08-24): a person can be part of Master Melittology WITHOUT being part of any particular atlas. Functionally they volunteer under the auspices of OBA staff.

This changes what the bead is about. 'No atlas' is not missing data to be chased down — it is a real, first-class membership state, and some of the 186 people currently without one are in it legitimately. The work is to let the model SAY that, not to reduce the number.

Two separable facts fall out, and conflating them is what the current shape does:

  MEMBERSHIP     which atlas, or the program itself with no atlas
  ADMINISTRATION who staffs them — OBA staff, for the program-only case

They are not the same, and neither is 'home_atlas = OBA'. A program-only volunteer in Nevada is not an Oregon Bee Atlas volunteer; OBA staff simply support them. Writing OBA into person_home_atlas would make them indistinguishable from a Corvallis regular in every listing, export, and eventual atlas-branded page.

So person_home_atlas as built cannot express it: atlas_id is NOT NULL, so the only way to say 'program, no atlas' is to have no row, which is exactly the value that already means 'not asked'. Absence must stop meaning two things. Shapes worth weighing — do not pick one from this note:
  • a membership facet that records the answer positively, with the atlas nullable and a kind saying which case it is
  • an atlas row for the program itself (rejected on first look: schema/010 defines atlas as 'a member program of the Master Melittologist umbrella', and MM is the umbrella, not a member)
  • keep person_home_atlas for atlas members and add a separate 'asked, answer is none' marker

Concrete consequences to design against:
  • Listings scope is mine / one atlas / all. OBA staff need program-only volunteers IN their scope, since they support them — but those people are not OBA members, so scope cannot simply be 'atlas_id = OBA'.
  • Atlas branding (beeline-2c3.11) has a clean answer here: with no atlas, MM acts as itself rather than on behalf of one. The brand model already allows that.
  • iNat project 99706, 'outside of Oregon', is the operational expression of this state and is admin'd by Andony — the same OBA-staff auspices, already true upstream.
Design decided (Peter, 2026-08-24), four answers plus what the dev store said.

WHAT THE DATA SAYS, which reframes the size of it:
- Sample-side absence is NOT ambiguous today. All 632 no-atlas samples carry a country and a state; zero unresolved geography. atlas_id IS NULL currently means exactly one thing.
- 'Outside the atlases' is mostly atlas members travelling. 469 of the 632 have a primary collector who HAS a home atlas (OBA 329, BC 107, WaBA 26, ID 7). Only 163 come from people with none.
- The program-only population is ~13, not 186. Of the 182 the overlay did not reach: 162 collect entirely inside an atlas (a roster-match gap - Lincoln Best, 338 samples, is in there), 7 collect in and out, 10 collect entirely outside, 3 have no samples. The 10: Roy Beckemeyer (67, KS), Coby Klein (15, NY), Kirsten Bovee (12, CA), Sara Dimas (11, AZ), Nikki Zebrowski (9, PA), Georgia Lopez (7, CO), Guillermo Fernandez (3, NY), Brissa Garcia (1, CA), Susan Boersma (1, AK), Peter Best (1, ON).

DECISIONS:
1. MEMBERSHIP is one current answer per person, not plural or historical. person_home_atlas becomes person_membership(person_id PK, kind CHECK IN ('atlas','program'), atlas_id, CHECK ((kind='atlas') = (atlas_id IS NOT NULL))). Row present = asked and answered; absent = not asked. Renamed because the concept widened - 'home atlas: kind=program, atlas=null' reads as a lie.
2. ADMINISTRATION is not built. 'OBA staff support the program-only cohort' stays a documented fact until there is a second administering body or a per-atlas staff role to hang it on.
