notes:
PARKED (Peter, 2026-08-29) until there is a need. Andony answered on gh-15: Carlson is a legacy edge case needing no code; households partition sample numbers by hand and he asked whether that could be encoded; Pat Wheeler should be asked to make an iNat account.

Two corrections the store forces, so the answer is not re-derived on the next pass:

PAT WHEELER ALREADY HAS AN ACCOUNT. person 63626, inat_account 793138 / patwheeler, 763 samples spanning 2018-2024 INCLUDING the 153 from the synthetic 9991048 block. He can sign in today. The issue listed him as accountless because it counted staging rows under the synthetic userId rather than reading the person table; asking him to register would mint a second account. Every other name in that twelve-row table is the same artifact: read as people, the 9991xxx cohort all stopped collecting in 2020-21.

'ACTIVE IN 2026' CANNOT CLEAR A TRAP COLLECTOR. The store holds zero trap samples dated 2026 -- all 10,771 of this season's samples are aerial net, against a dump current to 2026-08-16. That is entry lag, not retirement: Michael O'Loughlin (2,692 samples) netted on 2026-07-25 and his last trap sample is 2025-07-12; Dan O'Loughlin the same day, Henry Whitridge and Maggie Graham netted into Aug 2026 with last traps of 2025-08-23. Net records arrive through iNat within days, trap contents are sorted and entered a season later. So a recency filter silently excludes exactly the population this question is about.

Applying that correctly, the list before cutover is four names, all accountless and trap-dominant -- Heather Andrews (99 samples, 100% trap, last 2025-10-21), Mario Luppino (111, 90% trap, last 2025-09-17; 5,225 of his 5,544 records are vane-trap, his own collecting at scale), Salena Helmreich (21, 100%, 2025-05-20), Michael Getz (6, 100%, 2024-08-02). Every accountless person in the 2024-25 trap cohort is trap-dominant and every mixed collector in it has an account. Accountless and active in 2026: only Robert Pederson and Julie Biddle, both already holding delegation grants. Cleared and needing nothing: the 2020 synthetic cohort, Emily Carlson (last sample 2022, and Andony has settled it), Pat Wheeler.

The need that would unpark this: 2026 trap data landing for someone with no way in.

title: private.inat_oauth_token holds no token: rename it
description:
The access_token column is gone (2026-08-28) and the table still carries its
name. What it holds now is who has signed in with iNaturalist, when, and what
their avatar is — a sign-in record, not a credential store. The table comment
says so, which is the stopgap, not the fix.

Not done with the drop because the rename has an ordering hazard worth its own
change. attachPrivateStore creates any table its DDL file declares and does not
find, so renaming the table in schema/private/010_auth.sql makes a deployed
store CREATE the new name empty and keep the old one full — everyone's sign-in
history orphaned, silently. The rename has to run as an ALTER TABLE ... RENAME
TO patch that executes BEFORE the create-missing loop, which is the opposite
order from every patch in there today (they all run after it).

Doing it via the create path instead would also trip beeline-d34, since that
is the path that crashes on file-backed stores.

Candidate name: inat_sign_in. Touches schema/private/010_auth.sql,
src/model.ts, src/app/session.ts, src/app/roster.ts (hasSessions and the
lastLogin fragment), src/app/db.ts, and the tests that hand-build deployed
store shapes.
close_reason: Fixed in #122

title: inat:backfill-accounts binds accounts without recording it (beeline-o22)
description:
The person change log (ADR 0007) is written by legacy promotion, observation
promotion, the roster screen, and the app's boot reconcile. src/backfill-inat-
accounts.ts is the fifth writer of person data and records nothing.

It binds accounts — the sandbox reseed on 2026-08-28 watched it restore
Trinity Harvey (8386998/trinityharvey) and Philip Paterno (2758464/plpaterno),
whom the fresh promotion had left unbound. The safety net worked exactly as
designed: the app's next boot reconciled and recorded all four fields. But the
entries read `source=reconcile`, meaning "a pass noticed this and cannot say
who did it", when in fact a named job did it and could have said so.

Nothing is lost, which is why this is P3 rather than P2 — the difference is
attribution, not coverage. Fix is the shape promote-observations.ts already
has: call recordPersonChanges(duckdbReader(conn), changeLogFor(dbPath,
process.env), { source: 'inat_backfill' }) at the end of the CLI, and add
'inat_backfill' to CHANGE_SOURCES plus a label in the message catalog's
people.history.source map (a test pins the catalog against the union).

Worth checking at the same time whether any other writer of person, inat_
account, person_membership, person_admin or person_delegate is uncovered.
close_reason: Merged in PR #55: the backfill CLI records under source inat_backfill through backfillAndRecord, with the same gate and guard as promotion; other writers audited and already covered.

title: Token retention purge is documented but not implemented
description:
schema/private/010_auth.sql says of inat_oauth_token:

  'Retention is minimized: purge after months of login inactivity and on
   membership drop (scheduled job, beeline-2c3.4).'

beeline-2c3.4 is closed, and what it shipped was the SESSION purge
(src/app/jobs/registry.ts, "session-purge" → purgeIdleSessions). Nothing
deletes an inat_oauth_token row, ever. Found 2026-08-28 while adding
person_activity (beeline-dji), which wants the same retention rule and would
have inherited the same false claim.

So a non-expiring iNat access token for somebody who signed in once in 2025 and
never came back is still sitting in the private store, and the comment says
otherwise. That is the part that matters: the store's own documentation is the
thing anyone reading it would trust about what is retained, and it is wrong.

To do:
• A job that drops inat_oauth_token rows after N months without a login, and
  person_activity rows with them.
• Decide N, and whether "membership drop" is expressible yet — person_membership
  absence means "nobody has asked" (beeline-lcl), which is not the same as
  having left.
• Fix the COMMENT either way, so it describes what runs rather than what was
  intended.
close_reason: Fixed in #122

title: person.pronouns can only leave a deployed store by reseed
description:
beeline-6bw (9334a17, 2026-08-27) removed pronouns from schema/*.sql and from
src/model.ts, but wrote no migration, so a deployed store still has the column.
`pnpm db:migrate` on a store built before that commit applies 0010-0019 and then
reports:

  ... differs from schema/*.sql — a migration may be missing:
    not in the schema: person.pronouns

Found 2026-08-28 while migrating a copy of the dev store forward to test the
beeline-oyl delegation grants. The drift check did exactly its job (ADR 0006);
nothing else did.

Harmless in itself — nothing reads the column — but it is drift the check will
report on every run against the sandbox until it is resolved, which is how a
real divergence later gets read as noise. Either add migrations/00NN dropping
person.pronouns, or, if a deployed store must keep it, say so where the check
can stop reporting it.
notes:
CORRECTED 2026-08-28 (Peter): the remedy is a reseed, not a migration. DuckDB's
DDL cannot do this at all. Measured on a copy of the dev store migrated to head:

  $ duckdb b.duckdb -c "ALTER TABLE person DROP COLUMN pronouns"
  Dependency Error: Cannot alter entry "person" because there are entries that
  depend on it.

`person` is referenced by most of the derived layer, so there is no migration
to write — this is exactly the "no DROP COLUMN on a referenced table" already
recorded under ADR 0001's "Evidence since", now with a second instance. A
migration could only get there by rebuilding the table and restating every
dependent view, which is the derived layer copied out of schema/*.sql into
migrations/ — the opposite of the schema BEING the files.

So this is not a missing migration. It is a column that leaves at the next
`pnpm db:reseed` of the sandbox, which builds fresh schema and re-promotes from
the store's own staging. Until then `pnpm db:migrate` prints the drift line on
every run; it is a warning and exits 0, so nothing is blocked.

Two things to carry:
• The drift line is EXPECTED until the sandbox is reseeded. Anyone reading it
  before then should not go looking for the migration that would fix it.
• beeline-2c3.38's lesson applies to that reseed: db:reseed does not carry
  person_admin, so the admin roster rebuilds from the overlay alone. That is
  fixed now (the seed is applied per person), but the reseed is still the
  operation where a store's un-derivable state is the thing to check first.

Evidence for beeline-yfb, which collects the schema-evolution case: this one
cost nothing because the blow-away era is still on. After cutover the same
column would have no way out of the store at all.

title: Decide which is authoritative post-freeze: sample.specimen_count or count(specimen)
description:
Split out of beeline-daa, whose first half (the primary-collector invariant) is done as schema/116. This half genuinely belongs to phase 5, because it cannot be decided until a freeze exists.

specimen_count is documented as 'the working count: free to move up or down until printing freezes specimens'. Before a freeze there are no specimen rows and the count is the only truth; after one there are two numbers for the same thing and nothing reconciles them.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS. qc_rule_count_below_printed covers one direction — printed > specimen_count — and fires on 0 rows on the dev store. The other direction cannot become a check yet: count > printed is the NORMAL pre-freeze state, and pending_print_sample is built on exactly that predicate. So a symmetric check is not merely unwritten, it would be wrong until 'frozen' is a question the model can answer.

MEASURED 2026-08-28, dev store: of every sample that has specimens at all, none disagrees with its specimen_count. 66,294 samples, 380,279 specimens, zero divergence. Historical ingestion wrote both consistently.

WHAT CHANGED SINCE THE BEAD WAS WRITTEN. /samples/:id now prints both numbers side by side when they differ ('The sample is counted at 9; 2 have been individuated by printing', beeline-2c3.34). That is the first surface where a human sees the divergence at all — a partial answer to 'expensive to discover diverging after cutover', but a display rather than a check.

TO DECIDE. Which side is authoritative once a print run freezes specimens, and make the other derived or checked. A QC rule is a reasonable home, since a frozen sample whose count disagrees with its specimens is exactly the kind of thing a human should be told about. beeline-2c3.9 (specimen count editing) is an open write path into this and should not land before the answer.

Origin: the Symbiota archaeology gist, lesson 3 — every denormalisation is a permanent tax on every future write path.
close_reason: Answered by the build (2026-09-17, PR #74): the two numbers are different facts and neither is derived from the other. sample.specimen_count is the working count and keeps following iNaturalist up and down after printing (Peter, 2026-09-14). count(individuated_specimen) is how many places in 1..N a live run has frozen or the import supplied (schema/117; a canceled run's rows do not count). The freeze mints exactly the numbers in 1..count not yet individuated, and qc_rule_count_below_printed names the one disagreement that matters (count fell below what was frozen). beeline-2c3.9 (count editing) can proceed on that basis.

title: qc_rule_locality_format is 19 LIKE patterns over every locality (~190 ms)
description:
With the observation projection stored (beeline-2c3.36), this rule is the ENTIRE remaining cost of qc_finding: 187 ms of the ~205 ms union, with every other rule at 7 ms or less. It builds a space-padded, lowercased copy of all 66k localities and runs 19 'LIKE % x %' patterns over it to spot a street suffix.

One regexp_matches alternation does the same work in 15 ms — 12x, same 4,100 rows, verified on the dev store:

  regexp_matches(concat(' ', replace(replace(lower(locality), ',', ' '), '.', ' '), ' '),
    ' (road|rd|street|str|st|avenue|ave|av|drive|dr|boulevard|blvd|court|ct|lane|ln|county) ')

So qc_finding would go ~205 -> ~20 ms and every QC read in the app with it.

WHY THIS IS NOT DONE: it is an ADR 0001 portability call, and Peter's. There is no spelling that is both fast and dialect-neutral — all three candidates were tested against DuckDB:

  regexp_matches(s, p)  DuckDB: boolean. Postgres: returns text[], so a WHERE clause errors. Detectable break, one site.
  s ~ p                 DuckDB: FULL match (it maps to regexp_full_match). Postgres: PARTIAL match. Same operator, different answers, NO error. This is the dangerous one and worth remembering on its own — it is the kind of thing the beeline-l6w portability check should catch.
  s SIMILAR TO p        DuckDB returned false for a case that should match; alternation groups are not reliable here.

The existing comment says regex was avoided because 'RE2 lacks lookbehind anyway' — true of the reference implementation's boundary lookarounds, but the space-padded norm trick already removed the need for one, so a plain alternation is a faithful translation of the same semantics.

ADR 0001's evidence section already lists json_extract/JSONPath, list_contains and try_cast as construct families the Postgres hatch test found; this would add regexp_matches, in a QC rule view rather than in the ingest layer the ADR exempts. That is the whole decision.
close_reason:
Done (a471772). Peter authorised dropping dialect neutrality here.

The nineteen LIKE patterns are one regexp_matches alternation. 206 ms -> 16 ms for the predicate; with beeline-2c3.36 the whole qc_finding union goes 518 ms -> 25 ms on the dev store, one sample's findings 24 ms, printable_sample 32 ms. That is the QC home, both listings, printability and both record pages.

Equivalence was measured, not argued: over all 66,065 localities in the dev store (4,539 distinct) the two predicates disagree on NONE, and the rule's output is the same 4,100 rows with an empty symmetric difference — checked before the swap and again after migration 0018 ran against a copy of the store. The reference implementation's own false positives (St Helens, Lane County, Mosier St Park) are reproduced rather than quietly fixed; the space-padded norm supplies the word boundaries, so the alternation is a faithful translation of includesIllegalSuffix and needs no lookbehind.

Recorded in ADR 0001 as a named exception rather than left to be found: regexp_matches is boolean on DuckDB and text[] on Postgres, so a port rewrites this predicate and knows it must. ADR 0001 also now carries the  warning — DuckDB's  is regexp_full_match, Postgres's is partial, and it is the only construct found so far that answers differently in the two engines WITHOUT erroring. beeline-l6w (the portability check) should look for it specifically; that is the reusable finding here.

The old LIKE chain lives on in test/qc.test.ts, run against the new predicate over strings lifted from production staging, so the next edit to the token list has something to disagree with. Two more tests pin every token as a whole word and every near-miss (Drain, Avery Park) as not one.

388 tests pass, typecheck clean.

title: A record page costs a full qc_finding scan (~440 ms)
close_reason:
Superseded by the two beads that actually name the cost.

Filed when a record page's findings query measured ~440 ms and I assumed the whole thing was the un-pushed-down filter over the qc_finding union. Measuring per-rule showed that was wrong: the cost was never really the union shape, it was two things inside it.

- The observation projection, ~200 ms shredded on every scan and read by three rules — beeline-2c3.36, done (02d14b3). A record page is now ~200 ms.
- qc_rule_locality_format, 187 ms of the remaining 205 — beeline-2c3.37, open, and an ADR 0001 portability call.

The original point stands and is unchanged by both: the filter still does not push through the union, so a record page pays a full scan. It is just no longer the interesting number, and fixing it by reading anything other than sample_qc_finding would still be a second definition of 'what is wrong with this sample' (beeline-2c3.29). If beeline-2c3.37 lands, the scan is ~20 ms and there is nothing left to want.

title: Keep schema/*.sql actually portable: a Postgres apply check in CI
description:
[ADR 0001](../docs/adr/0001-duckdb-first-with-portable-sql.md) rests on
`schema/*.sql` staying dialect-neutral, so Postgres remains a real escape
hatch rather than a stated intention. Until 2026-08-27 nobody had ever tried
it. It was tried (Postgres 17.11, whole schema applied in filename order) and
the hatch is real — but it had already drifted, silently, because nothing
checks.

**What the run found.** All 23 tables, the `entity_id_seq` machinery, every
CHECK, foreign key and `COMMENT ON` applied unchanged. Four construct families
did not, in three files:

| construct | calls | file |
|---|---|---|
| `DOUBLE` (Postgres wants `DOUBLE PRECISION`) | 8 | `030_samples_specimens.sql`, `170_views_elevation.sql` |
| `json_extract` / `json_extract_string` with JSONPath | 20 | `105_views_observation.sql` |
| `list_contains(array, x)` | 1 | `105_views_observation.sql` |
| `try_cast(x AS T)` | 2 | `120_views_qc_rules.sql` |

The first is a plain violation of the ADR's own rule and is a search and
replace. The middle two are mechanical (`#>>` with a path array; `= ANY(...)`)
and are concentrated in the one view that shreds iNaturalist JSON, which is
where any engine's dialect shows most. `try_cast` is the only one needing
thought — Postgres has no equivalent, so it wants a small helper function or a
regex guard, and it is the pattern most likely to spread if unchecked.

So: roughly a day's work today, all of it in two files. That is the number
worth keeping true.

**What to build.** A CI job that applies `schema/*.sql` to a throwaway
Postgres and fails on the first error. It does not need data, the app, or a
Postgres dialect for Kysely — only that the DDL parses and the views bind,
which is exactly the claim ADR 0001 makes. Postgres 17 was already installed
locally; in CI it is a service container.

Worth doing because the drift is invisible otherwise: every one of the four
above was written by somebody following the rule, and the rule is only as good
as the thing that checks it. Related: [beeline-yfb](../.beads/) collects the
evidence for the re-decision this hatch exists to make possible.

title: "Last seen" on /people lost its evidence, and now silently means "last signed in"
description:
Found by an adversarial review of beeline-ten, refuting that bead's claim that
sessions are "disposable".

`private.session.last_seen_at` is the only read of session rows outside auth:
`src/app/roster.ts` uses it for the roster's **Last seen** column, taking the
greater of it and `inat_oauth_token.last_login_at`. AGENTS.md describes the two
dates as answering different questions — "`Last sample` reads from
`sample_collector`, and `Last seen` from the private store's session and
sign-in times".

The session rows were destroyed twice on 2026-08-27: once by hand during the
reseed (before the rekey existed, to stop sessions rebinding to the wrong
people), and again by the rekey's boot patch, which drops the table rather
than translating rows keyed on an id that had become untrustworthy. Both were
the right call for auth. Neither considered this consumer.

So `Last seen` now falls back to `last_login_at` for everybody. Tokens are
non-expiring, so a volunteer who signed in once in March and has used the site
every week since shows a Last seen of March. `/people` uses that column to
judge whether somebody is still active, which is exactly the judgement it now
gets wrong — and it gets it wrong quietly, in the safe-looking direction of an
older date.

Not recoverable: the rows are gone, and nothing else recorded per-request
activity.

Worth deciding:

1. **Does it self-heal?** Partly. Every sign-in from here on writes a session
   whose `last_seen_at` slides on each request, so the column becomes true
   again per person as they return. Six people had live sessions when this
   happened; everyone else was already answering from `last_login_at`.
2. **Should the column say which it is?** The roster prints one date from two
   sources with different meanings. A person who has never had a session and a
   person whose sessions were destroyed are indistinguishable from one whose
   activity really is that old.
3. **Should activity survive session deletion at all?** If `Last seen` is worth
   having, it is a fact about a person and not about a credential — arguably
   `person`-side, written on request, and then no auth change can take it out.
   That also removes the coupling that made this happen.

Low priority: it degrades toward "older than the truth", which reads as less
active rather than more, and the roster is admin-only.
notes:
FIXED 2026-08-28 (89ff9d6). Peter's decisions on the three questions in the
description:

1. SELF-HEAL — accepted as partial, no action beyond the fix below.
2. THE COLUMN SAYS WHICH IT IS, but only when it is the weak one. A visit
   prints plain; a bare sign-in prints "sign-in only". Same stance as the
   account chip beside it: the row speaks only where the plain reading would
   mislead, so the roster stays quiet and one column wide.
3. YES, ACTIVITY SURVIVES SESSION DELETION. private.person_activity
   (inat_user_id PRIMARY KEY, last_seen_at), throttled to an hour.

WHY A TABLE AND NOT A COLUMN, measured both directions before building:

• session.last_seen_at is written on EVERY authenticated request, unthrottled
  (cookieSessionResolver). It has to be: the 30-day expiry is measured from
  the real last request.
• It cannot double as the person's activity, because the idle cutoff is per
  credential. A phone in daily use would keep an abandoned laptop's cookie
  alive forever — that is a security regression, not a tidy-up.
• So the person-side record is an ADDITIONAL write, not a moved one. Throttled
  to an hour it costs one write per person per hour instead of one per request,
  and an hour is far finer than the only question asked of it.
• Keyed on inat_user_id, never entity_id — beeline-ten's own lesson, and what
  lets the row outlive a db:reseed of the main store.

DUCKDB DETAIL worth keeping: in ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ... WHERE, DuckDB
binds a bare identifier against the target table, so `current_timestamp` there
comes back as 'Table "person_activity" does not have a column named
"current_timestamp"'. now() works, and works in Postgres too.

Tests: roster.test.ts gains a private-store option and four rendering cases
(visit plain, sign-in qualified, visit wins over an older sign-in, neither);
auth.test.ts gains three through the real request path — the row is written and
keyed on the iNat user, it survives endSessionsFor + purgeIdleSessions, and the
throttle holds. The throttle test was mutation-checked (interval to 0 seconds →
it fails), because a timing assertion that cannot fail is not a test.

FOUND IN PASSING, filed as beeline-zg4: schema/private/010_auth.sql claims
OAuth tokens are purged after months of login inactivity, citing beeline-2c3.4.
That bead shipped the SESSION purge; nothing has ever deleted a token. The new
table states the same retention intent but names it as not implemented rather
than inheriting the false claim.
close_reason: person_activity records visits outside the session, keyed on inat_user_id; the column now prints a bare sign-in as one.

title: Two parse sites beeline-qcd inventoried and never surveyed: the identity fold and labelName()
description:
Found by reviewing beeline-qcd against its own inventory. That bead listed
seven parse sites and said the inventory was "to be completed as part of this
work"; it closed having surveyed scientific names thoroughly (`legacy_name_parse`)
and the shapes of `recordedBy`, `month` and `url` (`legacy_verbatim_shape`).
Three were not done, and one of the three turns out not to be a parse site.

**1. The identity fold** — `ingest/promote-legacy.sql:261`,
`regexp_replace(lower(n), '[^a-z0-9]', '', 'g')`. This is what decides that two
`recordedBy` spellings are one human, so its failure mode is the expensive
direction: two *different* people folding to one key and silently merging. The
reasoning behind it is recorded (typography must not split a human in two) but
the fold has never been run over the corpus and read.

Measured after promotion, no two `person.display_name` values collide — but
that is the wrong side of the merge to look at. The survey has to be over the
raw distinct `recordedBy` strings before aliasing: group by folded key, show
every group whose members are not obviously one person, and let a human read
it. `legacy_collector_duplicate_candidate` is the adjacent worklist and answers
a different question (people filing under one iNat login).

**2. `labelName()`** — `src/person-name.ts`. It decides the "P. Abrahamsen"
that gets **printed on a physical label**, permanently. It has 10 tests and, as
far as I can tell, every case in them is invented. It has never been run over
the 566 real people in the store and the output read.

Worth doing precisely because the interesting cases are the ones nobody thinks
to invent: 14 people have no `family_name` at all; nobody has a `label_name`
override set, so every one of the 566 is taking the derived path; and the
corpus certainly holds hyphenated names, particles (van/de/Mac), names already
given as an initial, and single-word names. A one-off script that prints
`display_name → labelName()` for all 566 is an afternoon's read and would
either find nothing or find something that would otherwise reach a pin.

**3. `verbatimEventDate` is not a parse site.** It is staged
(`src/load-legacy.ts:16`) and read by nothing — dates are parsed from the
`day`/`month`/`year` columns via `legacy_month`/`legacy_date`, whose failures
are already a `bad_date` promotion finding. `legacy_verbatim_shape` now counts
both. So the inventory listed a column that no rule consumes; nothing to
survey, and worth saying so rather than leaving it looking undone.

Both real items are read-and-decide, not build. Neither blocks anything; both
get more expensive after cutover, when the strings stop being re-pullable.

title: Morphospecies: 25 distinguishable undescribed entities collapse to their genus
description:
Found by the parse survey (beeline-qcd). 25 distinct morphospecies labels
across 88 legacy records — `Melissodes sp.1` through `sp.6`, `Stelis sp.1`
through `sp.7`, `Nomada sp.1`–`sp.5`, `Andrena sp.1`–`sp.3`, `Lasioglossum
sp.1`–`sp.2`, and singletons in Eucera, Megachile, Anthidium — all resolve to
their genus node and become indistinguishable from each other.

A determiner separated `Melissodes sp.1` from `Melissodes sp.5` on purpose:
these are entities they can tell apart and that have no name yet. The store
records "Melissodes" for both. Nobody typed anything wrong and no volunteer
can fix it, so it is not a QC rule and not a promotion finding — it is a thing
the model cannot say. `legacy_name_flattened` (ingest/parse-names.sql) is the
list.

Not urgent: 88 records, and the loss is now at least visible rather than
silent. Worth deciding before phase 7 sends these to Ecdysis and GBIF as bare
genus determinations.

Shape to consider: Symbiota puts `morphoSpecies` in the *unique key* of
checklist membership — a checklist can hold several distinguishable undescribed
entities filed under one taxon id
(https://gist.github.com/rainhead/7428e51bcbfc98108e191a7ec476a062). The
equivalent here is a `determination.morphospecies TEXT` beside `animal_id`, so
the determination is "genus Melissodes, the one I am calling sp.1" — with the
open question of whose namespace `sp.1` lives in, since one determiner's sp.1
is not another's. Related to beeline-tgu, which is the same shape for `cf.`
and `aff.`: both are determinations carrying more than a node id.
notes:
Andony, meeting 2026-09-11: the taxonomy for bees and bycatch is ITIS, and it already has been. That is the basis for volunteer determinations. How taxonomists handle morphospecies and similar undescribed entities is still to be decided, so this bead cannot be designed yet. ITIS has no node for 'Melissodes sp.1', so a morphospecies has to be either something the program adds on top of ITIS or a qualifier on a genus determination. That choice is part of what the taxonomists will decide.
Peter, 2026-09-14: how morphospecies are handled is DEFERRED. The related point (beeline-45v) is that verbatim determinations are preserved and not every one will resolve to an ITIS taxon, so a morphospecies name survives as verbatim text even without a model of its own.
Stale wording in the description: "before phase 7 sends these to Ecdysis and GBIF". Phase 7 now sends nothing automatically; staff download and upload by hand (2026-09-11). The morphospecies question itself is unchanged and deferred.

title: Atlases disagree about taxonomy — decide whether animal ever becomes authority-relative
description:
Peter (2026-08-27): there is some disagreement on taxonomy among the atlases.
Whether we will ever be motivated to model that divergence is not clear.

Recording the question and the stance now so the decision is made deliberately
rather than by drift.

**Today.** `animal` is one curated tree — one opinion, no authority column, no
`accepted`/`synonym` relation. `determination.animal_id` points at a node and
that is the whole story. schema-sketch.md leaves "versioning mechanics" open,
sketching git-versioned seed data plus an append-only `taxon_change` log.

**The stance this bead proposes: defer, and name the trigger.** Not because
authority-relative taxonomy is wrong — it is the right model, and Symbiota's
version of it is genuinely good: `taxstatus(tid, tidAccepted, taxauthid,
parenttid)` says *this name, according to this authority, is accepted or is a
synonym of that, and sits under that parent*. Taxonomic opinion is explicitly
relative to a source, which is how the domain actually works.

What happened next is the argument for waiting. `taxauthid = 1` is hard-coded
167 times across 49 files — search, synonym expansion, checklists, exports,
rare-species protection. The dimension exists in the schema and is essentially
unexercised in the code, so "unable to switch between thesauri in a checklist"
is a bug rather than a configuration. The gist's lesson 6:

> A modelled dimension that every query pins to a constant is not modelled.
> Grep for the constant before believing the schema.

(https://gist.github.com/rainhead/7428e51bcbfc98108e191a7ec476a062)

A second authority column that every one of our views pins to "ours" would cost
us the same and buy nothing.

**The trigger.** The moment this stops being decoration is when a second opinion
is actually being *read* — realistically phase 7, when Ecdysis and GBIF import
brings back determinations under names our tree does not hold, or disagrees
about. Until then, a divergence is a curation conversation, not a schema.

**What to find out first** (queued for staff, see docs/questions.md):
- Which taxonomies do the atlases actually follow, and where do they concretely
  disagree — is this a handful of contested genera, or a different backbone?
- Does the disagreement change what goes on a *label*, or only how records are
  grouped for analysis? A label prints one name; those are different problems.
- When two atlases disagree, whose name reaches Ecdysis/GBIF? Related to the
  open attribution question for records belonging to no member atlas
  (docs/questions.md, Printing and mailing 7).

Two smaller things that will matter whichever way this goes, and which the
domain needs regardless of multi-authority: identification qualifiers
(beeline-tgu) and a single source for rank (beeline-a2p).
notes: Andony, meeting 2026-09-11: the program's basis for bee and bycatch taxonomy is ITIS, including for volunteer determinations. This answers part of docs/questions.md 'Taxonomy across the atlases' Q1 for the program as a whole. It does not say whether individual atlases or outside experts (Ecdysis round-trips) depart from ITIS, and that departure is what this bead is about.

title: Two invariants nothing can check: sample.collector_id = collector position 1, and specimen_count vs count(specimen)
description:
Two denormalizations that are correct today and maintained by convention only.
Both are cheap to assert now and expensive to discover diverging after cutover.

**1. `sample.collector_id` is position 1 of `sample_collector`.**
schema/030_samples_specimens.sql says so in a COMMENT and then says why it is
only a comment: "an invariant promotion maintains, not a constraint the engine
can express." Three writers maintain it today (legacy promotion, observation
promotion, sample editing) and each new one is a new place to forget. If it
drifts, `sample.collector_id` and the collector list disagree about whose sample
numbering a sample follows, and the disagreement is invisible in any view that
reads only one of them.

Cheapest fix: a view asserting `NOT EXISTS (collector_id <> position-1 person)`
and a test that reads it after a full promotion. Worth also asking whether
`collector_id` should just be derived — the reason to keep the column is that
`sample_number` is scoped to it, which a view can express.

**2. `sample.specimen_count` vs `count(specimen)`.**
`specimen_count` is documented as "the working count: free to move up or down
until printing freezes specimens." Before a freeze there are no specimen rows
and the count is the only truth; after one there are two numbers for the same
thing and nothing reconciles them. This becomes live at phase 5 (beeline-1kb),
and beeline-2c3.9 (specimen count editing) is a write path into it.

Decide which is authoritative post-freeze and make the other derived or checked.
A QC rule is a reasonable home for the check, since a frozen sample whose count
disagrees with its specimens is exactly the kind of thing a human should be
told about.

Origin: the Symbiota archaeology gist
(https://gist.github.com/rainhead/7428e51bcbfc98108e191a7ec476a062), lesson 3 —
every denormalization is a permanent tax on every future write path.
`tidInterpreted`, `taxaenumtree`, `omoccurrences.family` and `omcollectionstats`
each generated a decade-long trickle of "X doesn't get indexed / doesn't get
rebuilt" bugs. Our structural defence is that determination-of-record,
printability and the QC rules are all views rather than stored columns; these
two are the places we did store a derived value, so they are the places that
need the check.
close_reason:
Split. Half done, half moved to where it belongs.

PART 1 — sample.collector_id = position 1 of sample_collector: DONE (f8110e8). schema/116_view_sample_primary_collector_mismatch.sql, in the same shape as determination_misplaced_qualifier and sample_elevation_stale, asserted empty after both promotions. It separates the three ways to break the invariant, two of which the hand-written check in test/promote-legacy.test.ts missed: a sample with collectors but none at position 1, and two collectors both claiming position 1 (which the (sample_id, person_id) primary key does nothing to stop). That test now reads the view instead of spelling the rule a third time. Migration 0019; verified against a copy of the dev store, where it runs in 2 ms and reports 0 mismatches across all 66,294 samples.

CORRECTION to this bead: it said three writers maintain the invariant (legacy promotion, observation promotion, sample editing). There is one — ingest/promote-legacy.sql. Observation promotion and sample editing do not touch sample_collector. So the invariant was in much less danger than the bead implied; the check is worth having before the second writer arrives (trap-sample entry, or any correction path that can add a collector), not after.

STILL OPEN, deliberately: whether collector_id should be derived rather than stored. Left alone because the column is a foreign key that qc_rule_duplicate_sample_number groups by and the roster's primary_samples counts — a refactor, not a cleanup — and because an invariant that is now checked is a much weaker reason to attempt one. Re-raise if a second writer makes it fragile again.

PART 2 — specimen_count vs count(specimen): moved to beeline-1kb.12, under the phase 5 epic, because it cannot be decided until a freeze exists. Note for whoever picks it up: qc_rule_count_below_printed already covers one direction, and the other direction cannot become a check yet because count > printed is the normal pre-freeze state that pending_print_sample is built on. Measured 0 divergence on the dev store today.

title: Rank has no single source: a vocabulary, an ordinal, and the italics rule live in three places
description:
`animal.rank` is `TEXT NOT NULL` with no CHECK and no ordering. Rank knowledge
is currently encoded independently in at least three places:

- `ITALIC_RANKS` in src/app/views/components/taxon.tsx:69 — which ranks italicise
- the deepest-rank CASE cascade in ingest/promote-determinations.sql
  (`legacy_expert_target`) — a hand-rolled rank ordering, in SQL
- the rank strings promotion happens to mint in ingest/seed-animals.sql

Nothing reconciles them. `src/model.ts` just says `rank: string`.

This is fine at two call sites and stops being fine at four. Phase 5
(printability, labels) and phase 6 (the determinations UI) each need "is this
determination at species or finer?", and today each would re-encode the ladder.
beeline-wn2's taxon typeahead will want to sort by depth. beeline-tgu's `cf.`
qualifier is only valid at species rank, which is another ordering question.

Proposal: a small `animal_rank` lookup — `(rank TEXT PRIMARY KEY, ordinal
INTEGER NOT NULL, italic BOOLEAN NOT NULL)` — seeded alongside the spine in
seed-animals.sql, with `animal.rank REFERENCES animal_rank(rank)`. Then "species
or finer" is `ordinal >= (SELECT ordinal ...)` in a view, the italics rule is
data the design system reads rather than a set literal in a TSX file, and
beeline-4zi's rank CHECK falls out for free as a foreign key.

Worth borrowing from Symbiota here: their ranks are integers on a gapped scale
(10 kingdom, 30 phylum, 140 family, 180 genus, 190 subgenus, 220 species, 230
subspecies), gaps of 10 so ranks can be inserted, defined per kingdom because
different codes genuinely have different ladders. The archaeology gist
(https://gist.github.com/rainhead/7428e51bcbfc98108e191a7ec476a062) calls this
the *good* part of their design — ordinal comparison is exactly the operation
the domain needs and it survives disagreement about rank names. The tax they pay
is ~150 bare integer literals scattered through the code with no named
constants. A lookup table gets the ordering without the magic numbers.

Depends on the same validation beeline-4zi is waiting on: a full db:build
against production staging, to see which rank strings promotion actually mints,
before anything constrains them.
close_reason: animal_rank(rank, ordinal, italic) added, seeded with the 9 ranks promotion mints plus suborder and superfamily; ordinals gapped by 10 after Symbiota's scale. animal.rank REFERENCES it, which subsumes beeline-4zi's CHECK. ITALIC_RANKS stays separate and wider (it must handle an unknown rank) with a test pinning the two to agree where they overlap. The ordinal has a caller on day one: determination_misplaced_qualifier (schema/115), the CHECK the engine cannot hold because 'species or finer' is a fact about animal_rank. Migration 0015; constraints on animal arrive at the next rebuild per ADR 0006, with a note saying why they get no stand-in view.

title: Admit a person from /people, rather than by hand-editing the curated overlay
description: The 'create' overlay field (beeline-2c3.32) has no screen behind it: admitting an intern or a coordinator means editing ingest/person-overlay.csv and running pnpm person:apply with the service stopped. Every other person decision is made at /people and written to the overlay by the app. This is the missing form — name, iNat login (verified against the API), and the decisions that follow — landing in data/person-overlay.csv like the rest. Waits until it is needed more than once or twice.

title: promoteLegacy takes ten positional paths: make it an options object
description:
`promoteLegacy()` takes ten positional path parameters. It was already at nine
and beeline-8t8 added the tenth, which is what surfaced the cost: four test
files now spell out three filler arguments at six call sites purely to reach
the last one.

    promoteLegacy(conn, TAXONOMY, "ingest/determiner-aliases.csv",
      "ingest/determiner-register.csv", "ingest/legacy-corrections.csv",
      NO_APP_CORRECTIONS, OVERLAY, NO_APP_OVERLAY, NO_ALIASES, REGISTER)

The filler is not noise, which is the sharp part: several defaults point at
files that exist only on a developer's machine — `data/legacy/taxonomy.csv`,
`data/legacy/usernames.csv`, `data/corrections.csv`, `data/person-overlay.csv`.
A test that omits an argument silently reads the developer's live data, so
every call site has to name every path defensively. Two of the existing
comments in those files say exactly that ("never the developer's live
data/corrections.csv"). The parameter list is what makes the hazard possible
and the filler is the mitigation.

Wanted: one options object with named fields, so a call site names only what it
overrides and omitting a path is not silently answered by the developer's home
directory. Worth doing before an eleventh input arrives.

Raised by an adversarial review of beeline-8t8 (2026-08-25), independently on
both the standards and spec axes.
notes:
Done. `promoteLegacy(conn, inputs: PromotionInputs)` — one required options
object, nine named fields, no defaults.

There are two named constants instead: `LIVE_INPUTS` in src/promote-legacy.ts,
which the ingest CLI passes and which is now the one place the gitignored paths
are visible together, and `FIXTURE_INPUTS` in test/helpers.ts, which every test
spreads and overrides one field of.

The hazard is closed rather than merely made visible. Omitting the object, or
dropping a field from it, is a compile error — verified both forms against
tsc (TS2554 and TS2741). Nothing falls through to a developer's working copy
any more, because there is nothing to fall through to.

Worth recording what the old defaults were actually doing: three test files
(legacy-corrections, promote-legacy-logins, sample-edit) were reading the real
ingest/person-overlay.csv, all 398 real people, because they passed six
positional arguments and the seventh defaulted. They now read the fixture
overlay and still pass, which is the proof nothing depended on it.
data/person-overlay.csv was the same shape of mistake but latent — the file
does not exist in this working copy, so `readOverlay` returned nothing; the
first staff edit made locally would have started feeding real overlay rows into
four test files.

Net -17 lines, and every call site now says what it is varying and nothing
else. 304 tests pass, typecheck clean.
close_reason: Closed

title: person-overlay.ts reads as binary to git
description:
src/person-overlay.ts contains a NUL byte — the separator in rowKey: `${r.person_ref}\0${r.field}`. It is the right separator (a display_name can contain spaces; NUL cannot appear in a CSV value), but git therefore treats the whole file as binary and every diff of it prints 'Bin 7888 -> 8307 bytes' instead of the change. Noticed while reviewing beeline-lcl, where a real edit to that file was unreviewable in the diff.

Fix is a .gitattributes line (`*.ts diff`, or `src/person-overlay.ts diff`), not a change to the key — moving off NUL would trade a readable diff for a collidable key.
close_reason: Fixed by da73ad4: a .gitattributes line marking *.ts and *.tsx as diffable text. The NUL in rowKey stays — it is the correct separator, since a space would collide on a display_name containing one; what changed is git's guess about it. Verified by re-rendering the beeline-lcl change to that file, which now shows the real diff instead of 'Binary files differ'.

title: Merge duplicate people in the roster
description:
Deferred from beeline-039 at Peter's request (2026-08-24): the roster does the other four management tasks; merging is out of scope for now.

Legacy name variants split some people in two, and the roster makes that visible without offering a fix. When it comes back, it needs: repointing sample.collector_id, sample.atlas_assigned_by, determination.determiner_id, sample_collector (keyed (sample_id, person_id), so a shared sample must collapse to one row at the earlier position), the 1:1 facets (inat_account, person_orcid, person_home_atlas, person_admin — survivor's own row wins), and private.session.person_id, which is a reference by convention with no cross-database FK: leaving it behind silently signs the person out, because the session resolver inner-joins person.

Two things learned building and then removing it:

1. It cannot be wrapped in a transaction on DuckDB <= 1.5. Repointing samples requires deleting sample_collector's rows, updating sample, and reinserting them, because an UPDATE is rewritten as delete+insert and trips the incoming foreign key; inside an explicit transaction the constraint check does not see the uncommitted delete, so BEGIN makes the very statement it protects fail. Verified both ways. The engine offers atomicity or the workaround, not both (beeline-c1b — retest when DuckDB moves past 1.5.x).

2. So the safety has to come from ordering: make every statement idempotent, delete the person row LAST, and ensure any prefix is a state that re-running the same merge completes. The overlay row asking for the merge stays on disk, so a retry is automatic on the next apply.

An overlay field 'merged_into' (value: a person_ref) is the natural shape, applied before the scalar fields so a later row naming the absorbed person lands on the survivor. The removed implementation and its tests are in the history of beeline-039.

title: 19 legacy people gain an iNat binding only at the next rebuild
description:
The corrected linking rule (beeline-eft, ingest/promote-legacy.sql) binds 19 people who the old rule left with no inat_account at all — their login was shared for data entry, so the old 'one login, one person' test discarded it. Verified in the dev store: old rule 390 rows, new rule 409, nothing lost.

Migration 0008 deliberately corrected only the three MISBOUND rows on the sandbox, not these 19 additions: a wrong binding hands one person's samples to another and had to be fixed today, whereas a missing binding only means that person cannot sign in yet, and granting 19 identity bindings in a migration without checking each against iNat is the same kind of unverified guess the bead was about.

They resolve on their own when the store is rebuilt before cutover (docs/roadmap.md). Until then a volunteer among the 19 who tries to sign in to the sandbox gets the pending-approval 403.

Do before cutover: re-run the list, spot-check a sample of the 19 against the iNat API (profile name vs person name), and confirm the rebuild binds them as expected. If the sandbox turns out to need them sooner, a follow-on data migration is fine — but verify each login first.

title: Listing flag chips ignore specimen-keyed findings; blocking_sample does not
description: Found by review, 2026-08-23. The listings' flag counts (src/app/listings.ts, QC_COUNT_SELECTIONS with WHERE f.sample_id IS NOT NULL) roll up sample-keyed findings only, while blocking_sample (schema/140_views_printability.sql) counts both routes — sample-keyed and specimen-keyed. Harmless today because every rule view emits NULL as specimen_id, so the two agree; the moment a specimen-level rule exists, a listing row can read 'clean' while printing is blocked. Two definitions of the same idea. Fix by having the listings read the same roll-up printability reads.
close_reason: Fixed by giving both sides one roll-up. New view sample_qc_finding (schema/130) keys every finding to the sample it belongs to — its own, or its specimen's — and blocking_sample (schema/140), both listings' flag chips (src/app/listings.ts), and the QC home's flagged list (src/app/server.tsx, which had the same defect and was not in the bead) all read it. Resolving the two routes with coalesce over a LEFT JOIN to specimen rather than a UNION also scans the qc_finding union once instead of twice: on the local 66k-sample store printable_sample went 1.14s -> 0.51s, and the listing roll-up stayed at 0.52s while gaining the specimen route. Same membership either way (60904 printable). Migration 0006-sample-qc-finding.sql; db:migrate --check clean against a real store copy. Regression test in test/listings.test.ts stands a specimen-keyed definition in for one rule view (qc_finding unions rule views by name, so CREATE OR REPLACE on one is enough) and asserts the chip and printability agree; it fails on the old code and passes on the new.

title: Name parts are lost when a solo collector's recordedBy spells them differently
description: Found by review of the 2026-08-23 promotion fix. legacy_person_parts now takes parts only where the recordedBy name equals the row's own name columns, case-insensitively: WHERE lower(c.name) = lower(concat_ws(' ', c.fn, c.ln)) (ingest/promote-legacy.sql). That was needed — otherwise 'Dot Other', named in a recordedBy on rows whose name columns describe Cy Ambiguous, inherits Cy's parts and a label prints 'C. Ambiguous' for her. But it is narrower than the problem: a solo collector whose recordedBy reads 'Pete Abrahamsen' while the columns say 'Peter' now gets no parts at all, so their label silently falls back to the full display name instead of 'P. Abrahamsen'. Measure how many people this hits in the real 383k rows, then consider a looser match (family name equal and given name a prefix or nickname) before cutover, when label text stops being cheap to change.
notes:
MEASURED (2026-08-23) against a clean rebuild from the real 383k rows — build + legacy:load + legacy:promote on current code, because the local store predated several fixes and gave wrong answers.

Blast radius is ONE person. 580 people promote; 15 carry no parts. Thirteen are the documented, intended cases (joint-only collectors, determiner-only records). The strict match adds exactly two:

- Pam Arion — the intended catch. Her rows' name columns say 'Mark Gorman'; without the guard her label prints 'M. Gorman'. Correct as is.
- Emily Hoskins — the bead's scenario, and the only one.

Recommendation: do NOT loosen the match. The proposed looser rule (family equal, given a prefix or nickname) would not even catch Emily/Emma — it is not a prefix and not a standard nickname — so rescuing her needs something as loose as 'family name equal', which re-admits the Dot Other class the guard exists for. And loosening papers over the real problem: 'Emily Hoskins' and 'Emma Hoskins' are two person records for one human (21 and 25 legacy rows, identical name columns, one holding iNat account ehoskins). Giving the phantom parts makes a duplicate look correct. The mechanisms for this already exist and are already planned: person.label_name for a one-off, and the curated name-parts register (beeline-8t8).

Deduplicating the person records is the actual fix, filed separately as the parent problem.
RESOLVED by beeline-eyk (2026-08-24). This bead's measurement found the strict name-parts match cost exactly two people their parts: Pam Arion (the intended catch, correct as is) and Emily Hoskins — 'the bead's scenario, and the only one'. Emily is now merged into Emma Hoskins by ingest/collector-aliases.csv, so there is no partless solo collector left to rescue. People with no parts fall from 15 to 14, and the 10 with samples are the documented joint-only collectors. The recommendation stands and is now moot: do NOT loosen the match — deduplicating the person records was the actual fix, exactly as this bead argued.
close_reason: The one case this bead existed for (Emily Hoskins) is merged into Emma by beeline-eyk's alias CSV. Loosening the name-parts match was the wrong fix and is no longer needed.

title: Listings show collectors in label form
description: Peter, 2026-08-23: the Collectors column should read 'P. Abrahamsen' — whatever will appear on the label. Done: the column renders labelName() (src/person-name.ts), which takes person.label_name when set and otherwise the initial plus the whole family name. The CSV keeps the full display name, because recordedBy in a Darwin Core export means the whole name, not the abbreviation a 3pt label has room for. The specimen listing's 'Determined by' column also keeps full names: that is attribution, not label text.
close_reason: Collectors column renders labelName(); CSV keeps full display names for recordedBy.

title: Flaky: promote-legacy sample ordering fails intermittently in the full suite
description: Seen twice on 2026-08-23, both times only under the full parallel suite and never when the file runs alone: test/promote-legacy.test.ts 'net and trap samples are distinguished by date range' got OBAS-00658 where it expected OBAS-00657 (the two trap samples swapped). A third full-suite run passed. The assertion orders by kind and sample_number now, so a tie is not the cause; suspect shared state between the files that promote the same fixture (each uses its own in-memory DuckDB, but they share entity_id sequences only within an instance, so this needs actual investigation rather than a guess). Reproduce with repeated full-suite runs before changing anything.
close_reason: Diagnosed and fixed. The bead's premise was wrong: the assertion did NOT order by kind and sample_number — test/promote-legacy.test.ts:89 read 'FROM sample ORDER BY kind', so the two trap rows tied on the only ordering key and DuckDB's parallel sort returned them in whichever order the threads finished. That is why it only ever failed under the full suite: solo, the file gets a quieter machine and a stable-looking order. Fix is the missing tie-break (ORDER BY kind, sample_number). Reproduced 2 failures in 8 full-suite runs before; 10/10 green after. Audited every other ORDER BY in test/ — the remaining single-key sorts are over unique columns, and the two other ties (promote-legacy.test.ts:67 determinations, :176 elevations) tie on rows that are identical in every selected column, so a swap is invisible.

title: Sign out did nothing under BEELINE_DEV_LOGIN
description: Peter, 2026-08-23: 'sign out does not sign me out'. In development, scripts/app-dev.sh sets BEELINE_DEV_LOGIN and main.ts then resolves every request to a stub session without consulting cookies — so POST /auth/logout deleted a session row nobody reads, cleared a cookie nobody consults, and redirected you back in. Cookie sessions (sandbox, production) were never affected. Fixed by marking the stub on the Session and having the account menu say what it is instead of offering a control that cannot work.
acceptance_criteria: A cookie session shows Sign out; a BEELINE_DEV_LOGIN session shows why there is nothing to sign out of.
close_reason: Coordinates now in both exports with provenance and geoprivacy beside them; dev-login sessions say why sign-out is absent instead of offering it.

title: Exports carry coordinates; downstream revelation is still the open question
description: Decided 2026-08-23 (Peter: 'why would we withhold someone's own coordinates from them?'). The listing CSVs originally omitted coordinates — my caution, not anyone's policy. They now carry latitude, longitude, uncertainty, elevation, the location source, and the record's geoprivacy/taxon_geoprivacy, so a row travels with what a reader needs to judge it. Rationale: a collector's coordinates are the ones they recorded on their own observation and the ones their labels print; 56,670 of 66,292 location rows are inat_public and already public; CONTEXT.md's stance is that anyone trusted with the main store is trusted with these. The blocker in docs/questions.md is unchanged and untouched by this: whether an atlas may reveal true coordinates of TAXON-OBSCURED records downstream — printed labels, Ecdysis, GBIF, any public tier. Revisit this entry when the atlases answer, in case an atlas wants its obscured records held back from in-app exports too.
close_reason: Coordinates now in both exports with provenance and geoprivacy beside them; dev-login sessions say why sign-out is absent instead of offering it.

title: Legacy specimen_number is now a per-sample ordinal, not the legacy specimenId
description: Promotion assigns specimen_number = row_number() within the sample (ordered by legacy specimenId, then _id) instead of copying legacy specimenId (2026-08-23, forced by merged collector spellings colliding on the UNIQUE (sample_id, specimen_number) — see beeline-vyq). Consequences: a sample whose rows were blocked or deduped no longer carries gaps, and a lone surviving 'specimen 3' becomes specimen 1. The legacy specimenId stays recoverable in staging (legacy_occurrence) pre-cutover, and catalog_number (fieldNumber) — the identity physically on the label — is untouched. Check with staff before cutover whether the legacy specimenId means anything to them beyond ordering; if it does, promotion should keep it where it does not collide and only invent numbers for the merged series.
acceptance_criteria: Either a staff confirmation that the ordinal is fine, recorded here and in schema/030 comments, or promotion changed to preserve non-colliding legacy numbers.

title: Two label batches under one recordedBy spelling: 20 legacy samples with overlapping specimen series
description: Found during the 2026-08-23 rebuild. Since collectors became a list (beeline-77j), name-spelling variants resolve to one person, so samples that were separate now merge — and 20 of them merge two legacy specimen series that both number from 1 (97 colliding pairs, 194 rows). Example: O'Loughlin, sampleId 1, 2021-07-31 — 'Michael O'Loughlin' specimens 1-4 with fieldNumbers 2120966-9 and Lasioglossum determinations, 'Michael and Dan O'Loughlin' specimens 1-10+ with fieldNumbers 2223231-40 and no determinations, same dateLabelPrint (31-Dec-21). Promotion now assigns specimen_number per sample so both series survive as distinct specimens, because dropping rows would lose the determinations and the two series may well be different bees. Staff question: are these duplicate label batches for the same physical specimens, or two real series? If duplicates, the dedup partition in legacy_ranked should key on the resolved person rather than the name spelling, and the losers become duplicate_specimen findings.
notes: Query to list the affected samples is in the beeline-77j follow-up discussion; they are all joint-collector spellings (O'Loughlin, Schelz/Maxwell, Graham/Whitridge, Larkin).

title: Health check should prove the store is readable, not just that HTTP is up
description:
/healthz (src/app/server.tsx) returns a bare 'ok' without touching the database. Because a single process owns the DuckDB store (ADR 0005), a wedged or locked store would still answer 200 — the listener is alive, the app is useless. Nothing watching the sandbox would notice.

Make it a readiness check: run a trivial query (SELECT 1, or something equally cheap against a real table) and fail the response if it throws. Must stay inside the interactive SLA and must not hold the store open in a way that competes with request traffic, so keep it to one cheap read.

Worth deciding at the same time: whether to keep the bare-text 'ok' body or adopt the shape from the expired IETF draft (draft-inadarei-api-health-check-06) — media type application/health+json with status pass/fail/warn and a per-dependency 'checks' map. That format is not a standard (the draft expired in 2021 and never became an RFC) but it is the closest thing to one, and it would give room to report the store and the attached private store separately. There is no registered .well-known URI for health checks — the IANA registry has none — so the path stays /healthz.
acceptance_criteria: A request to /healthz executes a query against the store and returns non-200 when the store is unreadable; a test covers both the healthy and unreadable cases; docs/runbooks/deploy-maderas.md's verification step still passes.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #41: /healthz executes a store read and fails when it throws; tests cover both cases; job staleness lives on /healthz/jobs.

title: Public tier on melittologist.org: what the atlases are, and how to join
description:
Scope clarification (Peter, 2026-08-23): melittologist.org carries TWO scopes. Beeline is the internal tool — session-gated, no anonymous reads. The public tier is the program's face: what the Master Melittologist program and its member atlases are, ways to learn more, sign-up funnels for prospective volunteers. These are different surfaces sharing a domain, so 'no anonymous reads' is a statement about the tool and does not preclude a public presence — an earlier framing of this issue wrongly treated it as a conflict.

Motivating observation: the smaller atlases have little or no web presence. New Mexico and Oklahoma have no site at all, only an iNaturalist project whose icon is a placeholder; Idaho is a Google Sites page. A public tier fills a real gap rather than duplicating one.

Several already-recorded future scopes belong here rather than to Beeline: the public-facing collector page, Canvas retirement's static content, and the CRM's prospective-volunteer funnel (docs/surrounding-systems.md).

Open, and not now: (1) whether the public tier is part of this application or a separate static site sharing the domain; (2) whether it ever reads Beeline's data — the moment an atlas page shows species recorded, the per-atlas geoprivacy question (docs/questions.md) becomes about a web page rather than about labels and exports; (3) its own voice and visual register, which the design system explicitly does not cover.

title: Signed-out page: links to the six member atlases
description: The sign-in page currently says only 'Nothing here is public — sign in with iNaturalist to continue.' Someone who lands there without an account has nowhere to go. It should link the six member atlases so a prospective volunteer can find their own program, and so the page says what this system is for. URLs and colorways are recorded in ATLASES in src/app/views/design/identity.tsx; the copy is volunteer-facing so it goes through the message catalog. Note NM and OK have no website — they link to their iNaturalist projects.
notes: This page is the seam between the two scopes (see beeline-58b). Today the entire handoff from the public world into Beeline is a sign-in page that tells an unrecognised visitor only that nothing here is public — no explanation of what this is, and nowhere to go. Atlas URLs and colorways are in ATLASES, src/app/views/design/identity.tsx. If the public tier lands first, this page's job shrinks to 'sign in'; until then it is the only public-facing surface the program has here.

title: Imagery policy: iNat photo display, attribution, licensing
description: /design/imagery currently answers only for avatars. Determinations (roadmap phase 6) will want observation and specimen photographs. Decide display rules, attribution requirements, and what iNat's licensing permits before any screen shows a photo.

title: Bespoke domain icon set
description: /design/icons states two vocabularies that never mix: Heroicons outline for UI chrome, and a bespoke set for domain meaning. The bespoke set does not exist. Candidates: sample, trap sample, specimen, label, determination, floral host, atlas. Designed by one hand, semantic not decorative, never recolored.

title: Project taxon.preferred_common_name for floral hosts
description: Decided at /design/names: the scientific name is the value, the vernacular assists (muted secondary line or title). schema/105_views_observation.sql projects taxon.name but not preferred_common_name, though it is present in the stored iNat JSON. Project it when a screen first needs to show a host.

title: Structured qc_finding.details so taxon names stop rendering as code
description: qc_finding.details is prose (schema/120_views_qc_rules.sql), and qc.tsx renders it inside <code>. For non_tracheophyte_host the detail IS a taxon name, so a scientific name reaches the screen dressed as a machine value — which /design/type and /design/names both forbid. Give details enough structure that the view can render a taxon name through the TaxonName component.

Structured columns detail_taxon_name/detail_taxon_rank on the rule and the union, rendered through a new FindingDetail component so both the dashboard and the sample page go through one definition. title: Master Melittology / Beeline mark: no logo asset exists
description: The repo holds no logo asset; the header brand is a text link and /design/identity ships a typographic wordmark only. Obtain the MM mark and wordmark, the per-atlas adaptations, and state clear space, minimum size, and approved colorways in /design/identity.
notes:
Two per-atlas adaptations arrived 2026-08-24 (Peter): New Mexico and Oklahoma, as 216x216 sRGB JPEGs from Adobe Photoshop 25.12 (Windows). Colours extracted and recorded on beeline-2c3.12 — that bead's colour question is answered for all six atlases now.

These do NOT close this bead. What is needed here is an asset that can be rendered at any size on any background: vector, or high-res raster with alpha. A 216px JPEG has no transparency and visible artefacts on the circular type, so it cannot sit on a coloured header or scale to a print label. Still missing: the base Master Melittology mark and wordmark (as distinct from the per-atlas roundels), the other four adaptations, and the stated clear space, minimum size, and approved colorways for /design/identity.

Useful as reference for what the adapted mark IS: a dark ring carrying the atlas name in circular type around an accent disc, behind a white bee whose abdomen is a map pin — identical construction across OR, WA, BC, ID, NM, OK. That is the shared program mark the brand model describes, so what /design/identity needs is one asset plus a colorway, not six separate marks.
Provenance lead (Peter, 2026-08-24): Karla Salp may have made the per-atlas marks. Peter is reaching out. If that is right, it is also the likely route to the source artwork — the base Master Melittology mark, the other four adaptations, and whatever clear-space and minimum-size rules already exist — rather than reconstructing any of it from rasters.

Decision (Peter, 2026-08-24): only real assets go in the repo. The NM and OK JPEGs supplied today are NOT committed — 216px, no alpha, JPEG artefacts on the circular type. They were used to extract colour (recorded on beeline-2c3.12, and that is durable regardless of where the files came from) and nothing else. The repo stays without a logo asset until there is one worth shipping: vector or high-res with transparency, with its origin and licensing known.

Ask Karla for, in rough priority order: the base mark and wordmark as vector; the six per-atlas adaptations as vector; clear space and minimum size; approved colorways — which would also confirm or correct the six ring/disc pairs on beeline-2c3.12, all of which are currently sampled from published images rather than stated by anyone.

title: Atlas colorways: the six real seed colors and per-atlas logo
description: Each atlas has its own color scheme and a shared Master Melittology logo adapted to it. Beeline currently generates one MD3 palette from a single honey seed (#b26a00). /design/identity proves the mechanism via /tokens.css?seed=..., but the real seeds for OBA, WaBA, BC, ID, NM, OK are unknown. Collect them, plus the adapted logo per scheme.
notes:
Eyedropped from published marks 2026-08-23 (approximate, UNCONFIRMED against any brand source):

  atlas  ring (dark chrome)      disc (accent = MD3 seed)   home
  OBA    #8c8c82 sage grey       #d23c00 orange-red         https://extension.oregonstate.edu/bee-atlas
  WaBA   #1e1e5a deep navy       #fab446 gold               https://agr.wa.gov/beeatlas
  BC     #6e001e maroon          #6eb4d2 sky blue           https://www.bcnativebees.org/bc-bee-atlas
  ID     #141414 near-black      #f0aa00 gold               https://sites.google.com/view/idahobeeatlas/home
  NM     not located             not located                https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/new-mexico-bee-atlas
  OK     not located             not located                https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/oklahoma-bee-atlas

Peter confirms colours and logos EXIST for every atlas — NM and OK simply have not been found. Neither runs a website; both are reachable only as iNat projects whose icons are stand-ins, not identity (NM's is a photograph of a bee, EXIF says Canon EOS Rebel T4i; OK's is a green state silhouette with a bumble bee). A null pair here means 'not located', never 'has no mark'.

Shared mark: OR, WA, BC and ID all use the SAME roundel — dark ring carrying the atlas name in circular type, bright disc behind a white bee whose abdomen is a map pin. So a colorway is a PAIR, not one seed.

Which half seeds the palette: the DISC. Verified by generating each: #d23c00 -> primary #af3000 (brick), #fab446 -> #825500 (gold), #f0aa00 -> #7e5700 (gold), #6eb4d2 -> #006783 (blue). BC is the useful case — its disc is sky blue, so the disc is the seed because it is the accent, not because atlas colours happen to be warm. Seeding from a ring would render Washington navy and Idaho black throughout.

Still needed: confirmed brand values for all six, NM and OK marks, and the cropped bee-and-pin glyph for small sizes (beeline-2c3.13).
NM and OK located (Peter, 2026-08-24) — the two 'not located' rows are filled, so all six colorways are now known.

Sampled from the supplied marks rather than eyedropped by hand (dominant-colour histogram over the whole roundel, page white excluded):

  atlas  ring (dark chrome)        disc (accent = MD3 seed)
  NM     #40b5a2 teal      6.2%    #fed700 yellow     4.7%
  OK     #323232 charcoal  9.3%    #841617 dark red   6.2%

Both confirm the shared-roundel finding: dark ring carrying the atlas name in circular type, disc behind a white bee whose abdomen is a map pin. Same mark as OR/WA/BC/ID, different colorway — so the pair model holds for all six, and 'a colorway is a PAIR, not one seed' is now checked against the full set rather than four of six.

Both discs generate usable MD3 palettes through the real generator (/tokens.css?seed=):
  #fed700 -> primary #6f5d00, primary-container #ffe169  (NM gold reads through)
  #841617 -> primary #ab332f, primary-container #ffdad6  (OK red reads through)

Note OK breaks the 'bright disc' shorthand — its disc is DARKER than the four previously sampled, and its ring is the lighter-feeling element only because charcoal reads lighter than #841617 at small sizes. The disc is still the accent and still the seed; the wording 'bright disc' should become 'accent disc'.

Files as supplied: 216x216 JPEG, sRGB, 72dpi, written by Adobe Photoshop 25.12 (Windows). Good enough to take colour from definitively; NOT good enough to ship as a logo asset (raster, no alpha, JPEG artefacts at the type). See beeline-2c3.13 — still needs vector or high-res with transparency, plus clear space and minimum size.

Provenance not recorded: Peter supplied them as files, no source URL captured. Worth noting where they came from before they are treated as authoritative brand values.

title: animal table: consider rank CHECK and UNIQUE (rank, scientific_name)
description: CodeRabbit suggested constraining animal.rank to its vocabulary and enforcing uniqueness of (rank, scientific_name), which seed-animals.sql's joins assume. notes: 2026-08-27: beeline-a2p proposes an animal_rank(rank, ordinal, italic) lookup with animal.rank REFERENCES it — which would give this bead's rank CHECK as a foreign key, plus the ordering that ITALIC_RANKS and legacy_expert_target currently encode separately. Both wait on the same validation: a full db:build against production staging to see which rank strings promotion actually mints. Decide the two together.
close_reason: Done as part of beeline-a2p. The validation this was waiting on is complete: a full db:build + legacy:load + legacy:promote against production staging yields 9 distinct rank strings and 0 (rank, scientific_name) collisions across 3,567 nodes, and promotion still produces 3,567 animals with 0 unresolved determinations with both constraints in place. rank REFERENCES animal_rank(rank) gives the vocabulary check as a foreign key rather than a CHECK; UNIQUE (rank, scientific_name) added. src/model.ts mirrors both.
